The one metric that wasn’t included when I joined the enrollment data with the organizational data is the number of years they attended a school in the Northeast region.


enrollment.original <- read_csv("/Users/kellyasche/Library/CloudStorage/GoogleDrive-kasche@ruralmn.org/My Drive/Research/FY25-27/FY26/OHE Journey to meaningful employment/Data/SLEDS/K12 Enrollment/K12Enrollment.csv")  %>%
  mutate(PersonID = as.integer(PersonID),
         K12OrganizationID = as.integer(K12OrganizationID)) %>%
  drop_na(PersonID)

k12.org.original <- read_csv("~/Library/CloudStorage/GoogleDrive-kasche@ruralmn.org/My Drive/Research/FY25-27/FY26/OHE Journey to meaningful employment/Data/SLEDS/K12 Orgs/K12Organization-updated.csv") %>%
  distinct(K12OrganizationID, .keep_all = TRUE) %>%
  drop_na(K12OrganizationID) %>%
  mutate(K12OrganizationID = as.integer(K12OrganizationID))

k12.org.master <- k12.org.original %>%
  select(K12OrganizationID, County, OrganizationName, DistrictID, SchoolNumber) %>%
  rename(county.name = 2) %>%
  mutate(county.name = str_replace(county.name, " County", "")) %>%
  select(K12OrganizationID, OrganizationName, county.name) %>%
  left_join(counties.regions.1, by = c("county.name" = "Name")) %>%
  select(-Dem_RUCA, -mif, -edr.simple, -planning.region) 

enrollment.org.ne <- enrollment.original %>%
  left_join(k12.org.master, by = "K12OrganizationID") %>%
  filter(project.pr == "Northeast")

n.years <- original %>%
  select(PersonID, grad.year, K12OrganizationID) %>%
  rename(grad.org.id = K12OrganizationID) %>%
  left_join(enrollment.original[,c(1,2,3,4)], by = "PersonID") %>%
  left_join(k12.org.original[,c(1,2,3,7)], by = "K12OrganizationID") %>%
  mutate(year = str_sub(TimeID, 1, 4)) %>%
  distinct(PersonID, year, .keep_all = TRUE) %>%
  group_by(PersonID) %>%
  summarize(n.years.attended = n()) %>%
  ungroup()

master <- original %>%
  left_join(n.years, by = "PersonID")

title: K12Orgs
text:
Summary of high school location
Lets breakdown the graduates by which RUCA category their high school was located.
Nearly 70% of the observations graduated from a county categorized as “urban/town/rural mix”, followed by 24.4% that graduated from a high school in town/rural mix counties and 5.9% from entirely rural counties.








Below is a map with the percentages of graduates graduating from high schools located within each county. This is the breakdown;

St. Louis: 55%
Itasca: 16%
Carlton: 15%
Aitkin: 5%
Koochiching: 4%
Lake: 4%
Cook: 1%

title: K12Orgs
text:
Summary of student demographics
The following analysis looks to see if there are any statistical differences due to rural-ness and geographic location of the high school for the following graduate demographics;

Were eligible for free or reduced lunch at some point in the dataset
Are Female
Have been homeless at some point in the dataset
Had limited english proficiency at some point in the dataset
Had non english speakders in home at some point in the dataset
Participated in a PSEO course at some point in the dataset.

The cross-tabs below indicate that there are 4 demographic variables that have proportions statistically different across RUCA categories. Each of the variables are indicated with an asterisk.

Free or reduced lunch: the more rural a district is, the higher the percentage of graduates that qualified for free or reduced lunch.
Homeless: as a school district becomes more urban, the percentage of it’s graduates indicating they experienced homelessness at some point increases significantly.
Limited English: the entirely rural districts had a slightly higher percentage of graduates with limited English.
Non-English in home: town/rural mix districts had a significantly higher percentage of graduates with non-English speakers in the home.
PSEO: a significantly lower percentage of graduates from entirely rural districts participated in a PSEO program.


RUCA Free or Reduced LunchRUCA FemaleRUCA HomelessRUCA Limited EnglishRUCA non-english in homeRUCA PSEO


Although 36.8% of the total number of graduates in the dataset receive free or reduced lunch, the more rural school districts had a higher percentage - 45.1% for entirely rural and 40.1% for town/rural mix schools.

k12.dem.free.lunch.ruca <- master %>%
  group_by(Dem_Desc) %>%
  summarise(n = n(),
           free.lunch = sum(economic.status)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(pct = free.lunch / n,
         total.pct = sum(free.lunch) / sum(n),
         data_id = as.character(seq(n()))) 

k12.dem.free.lunch.ruca.plot <- ggplot(k12.dem.free.lunch.ruca, aes(Dem_Desc, pct, fill = Dem_Desc)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = k12.dem.free.lunch.ruca$total.pct, color = "black") +
  geom_col_interactive(size = 5, aes(data_id = data_id, tooltip = paste(Dem_Desc, "\nTotal graduates: ", comma(n, accuracy = 1), "\nGraduates received free or reduced lunch: ", comma(free.lunch, accuracy = 1), "\nPercent of total graduates: ", percent(pct, accuracy = .1), sep = ""))) +
  annotate(geom = "text",
           x = 3,
           y = .4,
           label = "All graduates\npercent, 36.8%",
           size = 5) +
  labs(x="", y = "", color="", fill = "", title = "Percent of graduates receiving free or reduced lunch")+
  geom_label(aes(label = percent(pct, accuracy = .1)), show.legend = FALSE, size = 5) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels=scales::percent)+
  theme_line+
  scale_fill_manual(values= color.ruca,
                     guide = guide_legend(ncol = 3)) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom",
        text = element_text(size = 16))

  girafe(ggobj = k12.dem.free.lunch.ruca.plot) %>%
    girafe_options(opts_selection(type = "none"),
                   opts_toolbar(saveaspng = FALSE),
                   opts_sizing(rescale = FALSE))

k12.pseo.ruca<- master %>%
  group_by(Dem_Desc, pseo.participant) %>%
  summarise(n = n()) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(total.graduates = sum(n)) %>%
  group_by(Dem_Desc) %>%
  mutate(pct = n / sum(n),
         total.graduates = sum(n)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(pseo.participant = ifelse(is.na(pseo.participant), -1, pseo.participant),
         total.pct = sum(n[pseo.participant == 1]) / sum(n)) %>%

title: Pathways taken after high school - Northeast
text:
Attended Postsecondary Within First Year After High School Graduation
Key Findings
There is a statistically significant relationship between attending postsecondary within the first year after high school and post‑graduation outcomes across all timeframes:

1 year after graduation: χ²(4) = 6425.35, Cramer’s V = 0.370, p < .001, N = 46,777

5 years after graduation: χ²(4) = 1218.28, Cramer’s V = 0.187, p < .001, N = 34,683

10 years after graduation: χ²(3) = 259.34, Cramer’s V = 0.114, p < .001, N = 19,828

The effect is very strong in the first year and weakens over time but remains statistically significant. The central pattern is that those who attend PS in the first year are much less likely to be in regional meaningful employment, while those who do not attend are far more likely to begin working in the region.
Interpretation Over Time
Year 1: Students who did not attend PS within the first year had a much higher rate of regional meaningful employment (24.0%) compared to those who did attend (10.8%). Meanwhile, attenders were overwhelmingly in postsecondary (71.8% vs. 18.2%). This highlights the immediate split: PS attenders pursue education, while non‑attenders move directly into local work.
Year 5: Regional meaningful employment remains higher among non‑attenders (32.7% vs. 23.2%). However, PS attenders surpass non‑attenders in statewide meaningful employment (18.2% vs. 11.4%). Disconnection is higher for non‑attenders (25.7% vs. 18.0%), reflecting weaker long‑term stability.
Year 10: Regional meaningful employment continues to favor non‑attenders (34.4% vs. 26.6%). PS attenders retain an advantage in statewide meaningful employment (24.0% vs. 14.0%), while disconnection is far higher for non‑attenders (36.1% vs. 28.0%). This long‑term pattern confirms that early PS attendance pulls students away from regional work but enhances their broader statewide outcomes, while non‑attenders embed more deeply in the regional workforce.

title: Pathways taken after high school - Northeast
text:
Ever Attended Postsecondary (attended.ps)
Key Findings
There is a statistically significant relationship between ever attending postsecondary and post‑graduation outcomes across all timeframes:

1 year after graduation: χ²(4) = 21,822.13, Cramer’s V = 0.683, p < .001, N = 46,777【724†source】

5 years after graduation: χ²(4) = 4,066.08, Cramer’s V = 0.342, p < .001, N = 34,683【725†source】

10 years after graduation: χ²(3) = 372.88, Cramer’s V = 0.137, p < .001, N = 19,828【726†source】

The effect is extremely strong in the first year but declines steadily over time. The central pattern is that students who attended postsecondary are far less likely to be in regional meaningful employment early on, though they become more evenly distributed between regional and statewide employment later.
Interpretation Over Time
Year 1: Students who did not attend PS show much higher regional meaningful employment (19.9% vs. 13.3%). However, their outcomes also include far more disconnection: 44.2% “not meaningful” and 30.1% “no MN record” compared to 10.5% and 3.5% among attenders. By contrast, attenders are overwhelmingly in postsecondary (69.1%). This reflects a sharp early divide: non‑attenders attach to local jobs or disconnect, while attenders delay employment for education【724†source】.
Year 5: Regional meaningful employment becomes slightly higher for attenders (27.5% vs. 23.9%), and statewide meaningful employment is also stronger among attenders (16.5% vs. 11.7%). Meanwhile, disconnection is far more common among non‑attenders (27.4% “not meaningful” and 37.0% “no record”) compared to 19% and 15% for attenders. Thus, by five years, attenders gain more stable and broader employment outcomes, while non‑attenders remain more vulnerable【725†source】.
Year 10: Regional meaningful employment favors attenders (31.4% vs. 23.0%), and their advantage in statewide meaningful employment (21.1% vs. 14.4%) continues. Non‑attenders remain much more disconnected (41.7% “no record” vs. 29.2% among attenders). Long‑term, this confirms that attending postsecondary—even if not immediately—enhances both regional and statewide employment outcomes, while non‑attenders remain more likely to disconnect【726†source】.
Overall, the evidence shows that postsecondary attendance strongly reduces early local workforce entry but leads to more stable and broader employment later, whereas non‑attenders enter regional work early but remain at higher risk of disconnection.

text:
Attended Postsecondary Within First Year After High School Graduation
Key Findings
There is a statistically significant relationship between attending postsecondary within the first year after high school and post‑graduation outcomes across all timeframes:

1 year after graduation: χ²(8) = 27,442.69, Cramer’s V = 0.542, p < .001, N = 46,777【712†source】

10 years after graduation: χ²(6) = 408.26, Cramer’s V = 0.101, p < .001, N = 19,828【714†source】

The effect is extremely strong in the first year and weakens over time, though it remains statistically significant. The main pattern is that students who attend PS within the first year are much less likely to be in regional meaningful employment, while those who do not attend are far more likely to start working in the region.
Interpretation Over Time
Year 1: Students who did not attend PS in the first year had a much higher rate of regional meaningful employment (19.9%) compared to attenders (12.8%). Conversely, attenders overwhelmingly show up as still in postsecondary (74.6% vs. ~0%). Non‑attenders also show very high rates of disconnection (44.2% “not meaningful” and 30.1% “no MN record”). This reflects a clear divide: attenders delay employment through school, while non‑attenders move directly into local jobs or into disconnected outcomes【712†source】.
Year 5: Regional meaningful employment is somewhat higher among attenders (27.9%) than non‑attenders (23.9%). However, statewide meaningful employment favors attenders (17.0% vs. 11.7%). Disconnection remains higher for non‑attenders (27.4% “not meaningful” vs. 18.8% among attenders; 37.0% “no MN record” vs. 14.8%). Thus by five years, attenders are more successful statewide, while non‑attenders show weaker stability and higher disconnection【713†source】.
Year 10: Regional meaningful employment continues to be higher for attenders (31.6%) compared to non‑attenders (23.0%). Attenders also remain stronger in statewide meaningful employment (21.6% vs. 14.4%). By contrast, non‑attenders face higher disconnection (41.7% “no MN record” vs. 28.9% for attenders). The long‑term pattern confirms that early PS attendance reduces immediate regional attachment but supports statewide employment and better outcomes over time, while non‑attenders anchor more in the region early but face greater disconnection risks long‑term【714†source】.

title: Pathways taken after high school - Northeast
text:
Postsecondary Graduation (ps.grad)
Key Findings
There is a statistically significant relationship between postsecondary graduation and post‑graduation outcomes across all timeframes:

1 year after graduation: χ²(4) = 15,285.21, Cramer’s V = 0.600, p < .001, N = 42,459【736†source】

5 years after graduation: χ²(4) = 4,882.22, Cramer’s V = 0.378, p < .001, N = 34,144【737†source】

10 years after graduation: χ²(3) = 476.15, Cramer’s V = 0.155, p < .001, N = 19,828【738†source】

The effect is very strong in the first year, moderate by year 5, and still significant though weaker at year 10. The pattern shows that graduates are initially concentrated in continued postsecondary enrollment, but over time they transition into statewide meaningful employment and maintain somewhat stronger outcomes than non‑graduates.
Interpretation Over Time
Year 1: Postsecondary graduates are overwhelmingly recorded as still attending PS (77.4%), compared to only 19.4% of non‑graduates. Regional meaningful employment is lower for graduates (11.6% vs. 19.2%), while non‑graduates are far more likely to fall into not meaningful (35%) or no MN record (20.8%). This shows the early divide: graduates are embedded in education, while non‑graduates more often enter local work or disconnection【736†source】.
Year 5: By this point, regional meaningful employment is similar between the two groups (26.9% graduates vs. 26.3% non‑graduates). However, graduates are more likely to achieve statewide meaningful employment (18.0% vs. 12.6%) and remain more represented in ongoing postsecondary enrollment (27.4% vs. 4.2%). Non‑graduates are much more disconnected, with 27.3% in “not meaningful” and 29.6% with no MN record【737†source】.
Year 10: Regional meaningful employment slightly favors graduates (33.0% vs. 25.6%). Graduates also maintain a strong advantage in statewide meaningful employment (23.4% vs. 15.6%). By contrast, non‑graduates are far more disconnected (36.7% “no MN record” vs. 28.0% for graduates). Long‑term, this confirms that postsecondary graduation enhances both regional and statewide employment outcomes, while non‑graduates are more likely to face disconnection【738†source】.
Overall, postsecondary graduation is a critical predictor of long‑term stability, reducing disconnection and improving both regional and statewide employment, while non‑graduates remain more vulnerable.

title: Pathways taken after high school - Northeast
text:
ACT Composite Score
Key Findings
There is a statistically significant relationship between ACT Composite Score and post‑graduation outcomes in all three timeframes (ANOVA across outcome groups):

1 year after graduation: F(4, 27079) = 387.39, p < .001

5 years after graduation: F(4, 20617) = 159.11, p < .001

10 years after graduation: F(3, 10486) = 119.50, p < .001

The results show a clear and consistent pattern: students with higher ACT scores are more likely to attend postsecondary and later secure meaningful statewide employment, while students with lower ACT scores are more concentrated in regional meaningful jobs, not meaningful employment, or disconnected outcomes.
Interpretation Over Time (Tukey HSD highlights)
Year 1:
- Postsecondary attendees have ACT scores ~2.8 points higher than those in regional meaningful employment (p < .001).
- Not meaningful (+0.88) and No MN record (+1.43) also score above regional meaningful (both p < .001).
- Takeaway: regional meaningful employment is tied to lower ACT scores, while higher scores track into education and other categories.
Year 5:
- Postsecondary (+1.87), statewide meaningful (+1.84), and No MN record (+1.69) all score significantly above regional meaningful (p < .001).
- Not meaningful is ~0.62 higher than regional meaningful (p < .001).
- Takeaway: by five years, regional meaningful employment continues to come from lower ACT backgrounds, while higher scores predict broader education and statewide employment.
Year 10:
- Statewide meaningful (+1.64) and No MN record (+1.75) have higher ACT scores than regional meaningful (p < .001).
- Not meaningful (+0.43) is also above regional meaningful (p = .005).
- Takeaway: a decade out, regional meaningful employment is consistently tied to lower ACT scores, while higher scores are associated with statewide employment or exit from tracked MN employment.
Overall, the ACT Composite Score reinforces a strong sorting effect: higher scores steer students toward education and statewide jobs, while regional meaningful employment is more common among lower scorers.

High school accomplishments reveal two broad patterns:

2. Career and technical education measures (CTE achievement and course load) increase the likelihood of regional meaningful employment, anchoring students in the local workforce.
This split highlights the dual pathways of high school preparation: college‑oriented students exit the region or pursue statewide opportunities, while CTE‑focused students strengthen regional workforce attachment.

title: Pathways taken after high school - Northeast
text:
Total CTE Courses Taken
Key Findings
There is a statistically significant relationship between the number of CTE courses taken and post‑graduation outcomes in all three timeframes (ANOVA across outcome groups):

1 year after graduation: F(4, 45696) = 232.40, p < .001

5 years after graduation: F(4, 33828) = 104.15, p < .001

10 years after graduation: F(3, 19320) = 36.17, p < .001

The results show a consistent pattern: students who took more CTE courses are more likely to enter meaningful regional employment, while students with fewer CTE courses lean toward postsecondary, statewide, or disconnected pathways.
Interpretation Over Time (Tukey HSD highlights)
Year 1:
- Regional meaningful employment is associated with higher CTE course counts compared to postsecondary (−0.72, p < .001), not meaningful (−0.21, p < .001), and no MN record (−0.37, p < .001).
- Postsecondary students have the lowest CTE course counts, confirming that heavier CTE load ties directly into early regional work.
Year 5:
- Regional meaningful again shows higher CTE courses than postsecondary (−0.61, p < .001), meaningful MN (−0.44, p < .001), not meaningful (−0.33, p < .001), and no MN record (−0.45, p < .001).
- Postsecondary and statewide workers come from lower CTE course backgrounds.
- Takeaway: at five years, regional meaningful work is strongly linked to CTE engagement, while those with fewer CTE courses are dispersed across statewide or disconnected outcomes.
Year 10:
- Regional meaningful still has higher CTE courses compared to statewide meaningful (−0.31, p < .001) and no MN record (−0.31, p < .001).
- Not meaningful outcomes also show slightly higher CTE courses than regional (+0.21, p < .001), reflecting a mixed subgroup.
- Takeaway: a decade out, regional meaningful employment is still concentrated among heavier CTE participants, reinforcing CTE as a strong predictor of regional attachment.
Overall, total CTE course load demonstrates that increased CTE participation anchors students more firmly in regional employment, while lighter CTE engagement is linked to education and broader employment pathways.

title: Pathways taken after high school - Northeast
text:
ACT Test Participation (Took ACT)
Key Findings
There is a statistically significant relationship between taking the ACT and post-graduation outcomes in all three timeframes:

1 year after graduation: χ²(4) = 6187.26, Cramer’s V = 0.364, p < .001, N = 46,777【554†source】

5 years after graduation: χ²(4) = 1583.75, Cramer’s V = 0.214, p < .001, N = 34,683【555†source】

10 years after graduation: χ²(3) = 397.81, Cramer’s V = 0.142, p < .001, N = 19,828【556†source】

The strength of association is very strong in the first year and declines over time, but remains statistically significant. The key pattern is that ACT takers are much more likely to pursue postsecondary education, while non‑takers are more likely to enter meaningful employment in the region.
Interpretation Over Time
1 Year After Graduation: Non‑ACT students show much higher regional meaningful employment (19.8% vs. 12.1%) and are more likely to appear in not meaningful or disconnected outcomes (≈20% each). ACT participants overwhelmingly attend postsecondary (62.6% vs. 27.2%), illustrating a sharp divide between direct work and education pathways【554†source】.
5 Years After Graduation: Regional meaningful employment is still higher among non‑ACT students (28.7% vs. 25.0%), but ACT takers gain ground in statewide meaningful employment (17.8% vs. 11.3%). Postsecondary attendance is notably higher among ACT students (21.1% vs. 8.6%). Disconnection remains higher for non‑ACT (26.6% vs. 17.2%)【555†source】.
10 Years After Graduation: Regional meaningful employment narrows (29.9% non‑ACT vs. 28.6% ACT). ACT takers surpass non‑takers in statewide meaningful employment (24.2% vs. 13.9%), while non‑ACT students remain more tied to regional employment. Disconnection is still higher for non‑ACT students (33.7% vs. 31.3%). The long‑term trajectory suggests that ACT takers shift into broader statewide employment, while non‑takers retain a stronger regional employment profile【556†source】.

title: Pathways taken after high school - Northeast
text:
MCA Math (MCA.M)
Key Findings
There is a statistically significant relationship between MCA Math scores and post‑graduation outcomes in all three timeframes (ANOVA across outcome groups):

1 year after graduation: F(4, 42550) = 1344.53, p < .001

5 years after graduation: F(4, 33107) = 152.39, p < .001

10 years after graduation: F(3, 18728) = 94.98, p < .001

The results show an especially strong relationship in the first year, with effects tapering but still significant through Year 10. The key pattern is that higher MCA Math scores are linked to postsecondary enrollment and statewide meaningful employment, while lower scores are tied to regional meaningful employment and weaker outcomes.
Interpretation Over Time (Tukey HSD highlights)
Year 1:
- Postsecondary attendees score much higher than regional meaningful (+0.58, p < .001).
- Statewide meaningful is also above regional meaningful (+0.07, p = .026).
- Not meaningful (−0.06) and No MN record (−0.17) score lower than regional meaningful (p ≤ .001).
- Takeaway: early on, regional meaningful employment is positioned between low‑scoring disconnected outcomes and high‑scoring education pathways.
Year 5:
- Postsecondary (+0.28) and statewide meaningful (+0.27) both score significantly above regional meaningful (p < .001).
- Not meaningful (−0.08) and No MN record (−0.24) score below regional meaningful (p < .001).
- Takeaway: by five years, regional meaningful work is associated with lower scores relative to statewide and postsecondary, but still stronger than disconnected categories.
Year 10:
- Statewide meaningful (+0.29) remains higher than regional meaningful (p < .001).
- No MN record shows a mixed pattern: one contrast indicates higher scores (+0.13, p < .001) while another shows lower scores (−0.15, p < .001), reflecting sub‑patterns in this group.
- Not meaningful (−0.10 to −0.38) scores consistently lower than regional meaningful (p < .001).
- Takeaway: a decade out, regional meaningful jobs remain linked to mid‑range math scores, lower than statewide/postsecondary but higher than disconnected outcomes.
Overall, MCA Math reinforces the trend seen in other MCA measures: higher achievement channels students into education and statewide employment, while regional meaningful employment is associated with lower but not the lowest scores, positioning it as a middle pathway.

title: Final Wrap-Up: Pathways After High School – Northeast Minnesota
text:
This final synthesis combines findings across all four sections: Demographics, High School Characteristics, High School Accomplishments, and Postsecondary Experiences.












Section
Strongest Variables (Peak V/F)
Weakest Variables (Peak V/F)
General Pattern




Demographics
SpecialEd Status (V = 0.258, Yr 1); Race/Ethnicity (V = 0.126, Yr 1)
Gender (V = 0.109, Yr 1); English Learner (V = 0.062, Yr 1)
Demographic factors matter, but fade significantly over time; strongest for SpecialEd.


High School Characteristics
Avg. Unemployment Rate (F ≈ 53.1, Yr 1); Rural/Urban location (V = 0.094, Yr 1)
Range School (V ≈ 0.03–0.05)
Local economic conditions and geography shape outcomes; strong early signals that diminish with time.


High School Accomplishments
Took ACT (V = 0.364, Yr 1); MCA Math (F = 1344.5, Yr 1)
SAT Taken (V ≈ 0.07–0.08)
Clear divide: Academic/college-prep routes push students statewide; CTE anchors students regionally.


Postsecondary Experiences
Attended PS (V = 0.683, Yr 1); PS Graduation (V = 0.600, Yr 1)
PS Grad by Sector (V ≈ 0.14–0.16)
Postsecondary pathways dominate long-term outcomes, separating regional vs statewide employment.










SpecialEd Status and Race/Ethnicity stand out as the strongest demographic predictors, particularly in shaping early outcomes.

Gender, Economic Status, and English Learner status show weaker associations that fade quickly.

Overall, demographics set context but are less determinative compared to later factors.





Local context (rural/urban, unemployment, wage levels) influences early pathways, especially pushing some students into immediate work.

These effects diminish with time, suggesting that structural local factors matter most at the point of high school exit, but individual choices and credentials overtake them later.





Clear split between academic and technical tracks:

College-prep measures (ACT, PSEO, MCA, AP, SAT) → lead to postsecondary and statewide employment, reducing regional attachment.

CTE measures (CTE achievement, total courses) → tie directly to regional meaningful employment, with effects persisting 10 years out.


MCA Math in particular emerges as the strongest achievement predictor across all accomplishment variables.





This is the most powerful section overall. Postsecondary attendance and completion dominate long-term outcomes.

Attenders and graduates show stronger statewide and stable employment, while non-attenders and non-graduates enter regional jobs early but face greater disconnection risk long-term.

Institution type, credential level, and location add nuance:

Regional and 2-year pathways → strengthen regional attachment.

4-year and out-of-state pathways → expand statewide opportunities but reduce regional ties.







Across all sections, a consistent theme emerges:
- Regional meaningful employment is most strongly predicted by career/technical education in high school and regional/2-year postsecondary pathways.
- Statewide meaningful employment and mobility are driven by academic achievement, 4-year college pathways, and higher credentials.
- Disconnection is most common among non-attenders, non-graduates, and those with weaker academic/CTE preparation, compounded by local economic stressors.
In sum, the evidence highlights two diverging but equally important pathways:
1. Academic + 4-year trajectories → statewide mobility and higher credentials.
2. CTE + regional PS pathways → stronger anchoring in the regional workforce.
Both play vital roles in shaping the Northeast Minnesota labor market and should be considered complementary in policy and planning.

title: Final Wrap-Up: Pathways After High School – Northeast Minnesota
text:
SpecialEd Status and Race/Ethnicity stand out as the strongest demographic predictors, particularly in shaping early outcomes.

Gender, Economic Status, and English Learner status show weaker associations that fade quickly.

Overall, demographics set context but are less determinative compared to later factors.





Local context (rural/urban, unemployment, wage levels) influences early pathways, especially pushing some students into immediate work.

These effects diminish with time, suggesting that structural local factors matter most at the point of high school exit, but individual choices and credentials overtake them later.





Clear split between academic and technical tracks:

College-prep measures (ACT, PSEO, MCA, AP, SAT) → lead to postsecondary and statewide employment, reducing regional attachment.

CTE measures (CTE achievement, total courses) → tie directly to regional meaningful employment, with effects persisting 10 years out.


MCA Math in particular emerges as the strongest achievement predictor across all accomplishment variables.





This is the most powerful section overall. Postsecondary attendance and completion dominate long-term outcomes.

Attenders and graduates show stronger statewide and stable employment, while non-attenders and non-graduates enter regional jobs early but face greater disconnection risk long-term.

Institution type, credential level, and location add nuance:

Regional and 2-year pathways → strengthen regional attachment.

4-year and out-of-state pathways → expand statewide opportunities but reduce regional ties.

title: Final Wrap-Up: Pathways After High School – Northeast Minnesota
text:
Across all sections, a consistent theme emerges:
- Regional meaningful employment is most strongly predicted by career/technical education in high school and regional/2-year postsecondary pathways.
- Statewide meaningful employment and mobility are driven by academic achievement, 4-year college pathways, and higher credentials.
- Disconnection is most common among non-attenders, non-graduates, and those with weaker academic/CTE preparation, compounded by local economic stressors.
In sum, the evidence highlights two diverging but equally important pathways:
1. Academic + 4-year trajectories → statewide mobility and higher credentials.
2. CTE + regional PS pathways → stronger anchoring in the regional workforce.
Both play vital roles in shaping the Northeast Minnesota labor market and should be considered complementary in policy and planning.

title: Pathways taken after high school - Northeast
text:
Average County Wages as Percent of State (Sophomore–Senior Years)
Key Findings
There is a statistically significant relationship between relative county wages and post‑graduation outcomes in all three timeframes (ANOVA on wage percent across outcome groups):

1 year after graduation: F(4, 46751) = 15.33, p < .001

5 years after graduation: F(4, 34678) = 24.64, p < .001

10 years after graduation: F(3, 19824) = 11.82, p < .001

Although effect sizes are small, the relationships are consistent. The primary finding is that graduates from counties with higher relative wages are more likely to pursue postsecondary education, while those from lower‑wage counties are more likely to be in meaningful regional employment.
Interpretation Over Time (Tukey HSD highlights)
Year 1:
- Postsecondary attendees come from higher‑wage counties than nearly all other groups (Δ ≈ +0.009 vs. regional meaningful, p < .001).
- Not meaningful and No MN record are also slightly higher than regional meaningful (Δ ≈ +0.006–0.008, p ≤ .05).
- Takeaway: early on, regional meaningful employment is linked to lower‑wage counties, while education is linked to higher‑wage contexts.
Year 5:
- Postsecondary attendees again come from higher‑wage counties (+0.009 vs. meaningful MN, p < .001).
- Regional meaningful employment is associated with lower‑wage contexts compared to statewide meaningful (Δ = −0.009, p < .001).
- Not meaningful and No MN record are slightly higher than regional meaningful (Δ ≈ +0.005–0.006, both p < .01).
- Takeaway: statewide meaningful employment and further schooling are linked to higher‑wage counties, while regional meaningful work remains concentrated in lower‑wage areas.
Year 10:
- Regional meaningful employment continues to be tied to lower‑wage counties than statewide meaningful (Δ = −0.007, p < .001).
- Not meaningful (+0.004, p = .008) and No MN record (+0.006, p < .001) are also above regional meaningful.
- Takeaway: a decade out, the pattern solidifies — regional meaningful employment is most strongly associated with lower‑wage counties, while higher‑wage counties are more tied to education, statewide meaningful, or disconnected pathways.
Overall, the wage context shows a consistent divide: regional meaningful jobs are concentrated in lower‑wage counties, whereas higher‑wage counties foster postsecondary and statewide pathways.

title: Pathways taken after high school - Northeast
text:
High School Rural–Urban Context (Dem_Desc)
Key Findings
There is a statistically significant relationship between rural–urban context and post-graduation outcomes in all three timeframes:

1 year after graduation: χ²(8) = 54.72, Cramer’s V = 0.024, p < .001, N = 46,777【474†source】

5 years after graduation: χ²(8) = 201.14, Cramer’s V = 0.054, p < .001, N = 34,683【476†source】

10 years after graduation: χ²(6) = 75.40, Cramer’s V = 0.044, p < .001, N = 19,828【477†source】

The associations are weak but consistent. The primary pattern is that students from Urban/town/rural mix areas are most likely to achieve meaningful employment in the region, while those from Entirely rural areas are least likely to do so, especially by Years 5 and 10.
Interpretation Over Time
1 Year After Graduation: Regional meaningful employment is highest for Urban/town/rural mix (15.8%), followed by Town/rural mix (14.9%), and lowest for Entirely rural (11.8%). Postsecondary attendance is nearly identical across groups (~48%). Disconnection is slightly higher for Entirely rural (12.1%) compared to others (≈11.6–11.9%)【474†source】.
5 Years After Graduation: Urban/town/rural mix leads in regional meaningful employment (27.8%), compared to Town/rural mix (24.3%) and Entirely rural (20.2%). Interestingly, Entirely rural graduates show higher statewide meaningful employment (23.5%), indicating more attachment to jobs outside their immediate region. Disconnection is modestly lower for Entirely rural (19.7%) compared to others (≈20.8–21.9%)【476†source】.
10 Years After Graduation: The pattern persists. Urban/town/rural mix maintains the highest regional meaningful employment (30.3%), while Entirely rural remains lowest (22.8%). Entirely rural students, however, hold the highest statewide meaningful employment share (26.9%), reinforcing the pattern of outward mobility for work. Disconnection is high across all groups (~30–33%) but does not vary sharply by rural–urban context【477†source】.
Overall, the rural–urban context shows weak but clear differences: students from more urban-influenced areas are more likely to remain in meaningful employment within the region, while those from entirely rural schools are more likely to find meaningful employment elsewhere in Minnesota.

title: Pathways taken after high school - Northeast
text:
English Learner Status
Key Findings
There is a statistically significant relationship between English Learner (EL) status and post-graduation outcomes in all three timeframes:

1 year after graduation: χ²(4) = 1649.35, Cramer’s V = 0.188, p < .001, N = 46,777【448†source】

5 years after graduation: χ²(4) = 459.23, Cramer’s V = 0.115, p < .001, N = 34,683【449†source】

10 years after graduation: χ²(3) = 124.44, Cramer’s V = 0.079, p < .001, N = 19,828【450†source】

The strength of association is strongest in the first year and weakens over time, though the relationship remains significant. The primary relationship is that English Learner students are much less likely to attend postsecondary and more likely to be disconnected or in not meaningful employment, while non-EL students are more likely to pursue postsecondary and secure meaningful regional employment over time.
Interpretation Over Time
1 Year After Graduation: Non-EL students are more likely to be attending postsecondary (49.2% vs. 16.6%) and in meaningful regional employment (15.5% vs. 11.8%). EL students are disproportionately represented in not meaningful (31.8% vs. 20.4%) and disconnected outcomes (35.8% vs. 10.6%). This shows a sharp early divide.
5 Years After Graduation: Regional meaningful employment grows for both groups, but the gap persists (26.7% non-EL vs. 21.1% EL). EL students continue to be much less likely to be in postsecondary (3.7% vs. 16.6%) and more likely to be disconnected (38.1% vs. 20.3%). By this point, EL students are more than 15 percentage points less likely to secure regional meaningful jobs.
10 Years After Graduation: Non-EL students further strengthen their advantage in meaningful regional employment (29.6% vs. 17.4%) and statewide meaningful employment (19.7% vs. 7.6%). Nearly half of EL students (48.3%) remain disconnected, compared to 32.0% of non-EL students. The long-term trajectory shows that English Learners face enduring disadvantages in both education and attachment to meaningful regional employment.

title: Pathways taken after high school - Northeast
text:
Race/Ethnicity
Key Findings
There is a statistically significant relationship between race/ethnicity and post-graduation outcomes in all three timeframes:

1 year after graduation: χ²(16) = 737.61, Cramer’s V = 0.067, p < .001, N = 41,205【435†source】

5 years after graduation: χ²(16) = 363.79, Cramer’s V = 0.051, p < .001, N = 34,683【437†source】

10 years after graduation: χ²(12) = 198.54, Cramer’s V = 0.058, p < .001, N = 19,828【438†source】

The associations are weak but consistent across time, suggesting that while race/ethnicity matters, the effect sizes are smaller compared to other demographic variables. The primary relationship is that White students are more likely to enter meaningful regional employment and attend postsecondary, while American Indian, Black, and Hispanic students are more often in not meaningful or disconnected outcomes.
Interpretation Over Time
1 Year After Graduation: White students show higher rates of postsecondary attendance (50.1%) and meaningful regional employment (15.3%) compared to most other groups. American Indian students are less likely to attend postsecondary (32.2%) and more likely to be in not meaningful employment (28.8%) or disconnected (18.7%). Black and Hispanic students also face higher shares of not meaningful or disconnected outcomes, while Asian/PI students lean toward postsecondary enrollment (48.1%) but have low regional employment (8.3%).
5 Years After Graduation: White students continue to dominate in meaningful regional employment (27.1%) and statewide meaningful work (15.6%). American Indian, Black, and Hispanic students remain underrepresented in regional employment (15.9–19.8%) and have higher shares in not meaningful or disconnected outcomes. Asian/PI students, though still lower in regional employment (15.9%), maintain stronger postsecondary presence (18.9%). The disparities remain persistent.
10 Years After Graduation: White students further strengthen their advantage in meaningful regional employment (30.1%) and statewide meaningful work (19.9%). American Indian, Black, and Hispanic students remain behind, with regional employment in the 13–21% range and higher disconnection rates (44–50% for Black and Hispanic). Asian/PI students continue to have weaker attachment to regional employment (15.6%), though they retain moderate statewide meaningful employment. The long-term pattern highlights systemic disparities in both education and labor market outcomes, with White students benefiting most from regional meaningful employment opportunities.

The original dataset provides whether the student was a basic participant, basic concentrator, basic completor, and/or a centrentrator 150 when taking a CTE course. It looks like each observation is unique by grade of the student. This means that one PersonID can have multiple observations.
In order to determine how I want to organize this data so that each observation represents the full characteristics of each PersonID I need to understand how these values are defined.

Basic Participant: Any grade 9-12 student who successfully completes one or more state-approved CTE course(s).
Basic Concentrator: this is the old standard for years and required the student complete 240 hours. Any student successfully enrolled in a single CTE field for more than 240 hours (successful is defined as passing grade).
Basic Completor: any concentrator who attains academic and technical knowledge and skills and graduates from high school.
Concentrator 150: This is the new standard - Any grade 9-12 student who successfully completes 150+ course hours (or more) as part of a state-approved secondary CTE program, within one career field.

Judging by these definitions, it seems that we will want three categories;

Those that participated in a CTE course but were not a concentrator or a completor, and
Those that participated in a CTE course and graduated as a concentrator.
Those that did not participate in a CTE course.

So essentially, filtering this dataset to provide the “highest level achieved” in terms of CTE coursework. We will focus on filtering this dataset to the highest level achieved and will then join with the graduate list which will have all the individuals that did not participate in any CTE courses.


graduate <- read_csv("Data/SLEDS/Masters/Master-4.csv") %>%
  select(PersonID)

cte.concentrator.cat <- cte.demographics.original %>%
  gather(key = "cte.achievement", value = "yes.or.no", 4:7) %>%
  filter(yes.or.no != "Null") %>%
  filter(yes.or.no != "NULL") %>%
  filter(yes.or.no != "N") %>%
  mutate(cte.achievement = as.factor(cte.achievement),
         yes.or.no = as.factor(yes.or.no),
         cte.achievement.code = ifelse(cte.achievement == "BasicParticipant", 0, 1)) %>%
  select(PersonID, cte.achievement, cte.achievement.code) %>%
  group_by(PersonID) %>%
  summarise(cte.achievement.code = sum(cte.achievement.code)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(cte.achievement = ifelse(cte.achievement.code == 0, "CTE Participant", "CTE Concentrator or Completor")) %>%
  select(PersonID, cte.achievement) %>%
  right_join(graduate, by = "PersonID") %>%
  mutate(cte.achievement = ifelse(is.na(cte.achievement), "No CTE", cte.achievement))

text:
The next dataset is individuals that were enrolled in CTE courses. I’m first going to load the entire dataset, then clean it up, and then I will merge it with my master/NE graduate dataset.


cte.enrollment.original <- read_csv('/Users/kellyasche/Library/CloudStorage/GoogleDrive-kasche@ruralmn.org/My Drive/Research/FY25-27/FY26/OHE Journey to meaningful employment/Data/SLEDS/CTEEnrollment/CTEEnrollment.csv') %>%
  mutate(PersonID = as.integer(PersonID)) %>%
  filter(FiscalYearTimeID != "NULL") %>%
  mutate(CareerCluster = ifelse(CareerCluster == "26" & CareerClusterName == "Diversified Youth Apprenticeship", "25", CareerCluster),
         CareerCluster = ifelse(CareerCluster == "NULL", "0", CareerCluster),
         CareerCluster = str_replace(CareerCluster, "Design", "11"),
         CareerCluster = as.integer(CareerCluster))


career.cluster.codes.names.original <- read_xlsx('/Users/kellyasche/Library/CloudStorage/GoogleDrive-kasche@ruralmn.org/My Drive/Research/FY25-27/FY26/OHE Journey to meaningful employment/Data/SLEDS/CTEEnrollment/career-cluster-codes-names_from SLEDS_March2025.xlsx') %>%
  mutate(cte.year = ifelse(Introduced > 2020, 2021, Discontinued),
         cte.year = ifelse(is.na(Introduced) & is.na(Discontinued), 2021, cte.year),
         cte.year = ifelse(is.na(cte.year), 2020, cte.year),
         CareerClusterName.new = as_factor(CareerClusterName.new))


career.cluster.codes.names.addendum <- data.frame(`CareerCluster` = c(0, 1, 2),
                                                  CareerClusterName.new = c("NULL", "Agriculture, Food, and Natural Resources", "Architecture & Construction"),
                                                  Status = c("Retired", "Retired", "Retired"),
                                                  Introduced = c(2021, 2021, 2021),
                                                  Discontinued = c(2021, 2021, 2021),
                                                  cte.year = c(2020, 2020, 2020))

career.cluster.codes.names <- career.cluster.codes.names.original %>%
  rbind(career.cluster.codes.names.addendum)

cte.enrollment.master <- cte.enrollment.original %>%
  mutate(year = str_sub(FiscalYearTimeID, 1, 4),
         year = as.integer(year),
         cte.year = ifelse(year < 2021, 2020, 2021)) %>%
  left_join(career.cluster.codes.names[,c(1,2,6)], by = c("CareerCluster", "cte.year")) %>%
  select(-CareerClusterName, -year, -cte.year) %>%
  rename(CareerClusterName = CareerClusterName.new)

This dataset provides each CTE course taken by a student. This means that there were 1,956,574 instances of a student taking a CTE course. There are 12 columns providing the PersonID taking the course, the fiscal year, the K12 organization, along with details about the actual course itself.
There are two goals with this dataset.

Format it so each observation represents a single PersonID along with the total number of CTE courses they took.
Format it so each observation represents a single PersonID along with the number of CTE courses taken in each CareerCluster.

I’m using careerclusters due to their specificity.

  group_by(PersonID) %>%
  summarise(total.cte.courses.taken = n()) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  right_join(graduate, by = "PersonID") %>%
  mutate(total.cte.courses.taken = ifelse(is.na(total.cte.courses.taken), 0, total.cte.courses.taken))

There seems to be a minor coding error in the careercluster column. For one particular class, it was consistently labeled “Information Technology” even though the field requires a number value. In addition, “information Technology” doesn’t seem to match the course due to the following information;
Program Course Name: Family and Consumer Science Course title: Apparrel CareerCluster: Design CareerClusterName: 6 (which should be a letter value, not a code).
Due to this information, I recoded anything that was “Information Technology” for that particular course as a “6”.
In addition, there were some errors in careercluster 26, which is supposed to be “Administrative only” but had a number of “Youth Apprenticeships” in it that I recoded to CareerCluster 25.

title: CTEEnrollment
section: Summary - Number of CTE courses taken by a student
text:
Summary - Number of CTE courses taken by a student

We’ll start with summarising the number of cte courses the observations have taken.
The tables below show that the average number of CTE courses taken by all PersonID in the master dataset is 2.29 with a standard deviation of +/-2.39. This is a high standard deviation meaning there are values quite far from the mean.
The second row of the table shows the average number of CTE courses taken by individuals who took at least one CTE course. The average jumps up a bit to 3.20 with a standard deviation of 2.25.


cte.n.courses.summary.total <- master.4 %>%
  summarise(mean = mean(total.cte.courses.taken),
            median = median(total.cte.courses.taken),
            sd = sd(total.cte.courses.taken),
            n = comma(n(), accuracy = 1),
            min = min(total.cte.courses.taken),
            max = max(total.cte.courses.taken)) %>%
  mutate(population = "All graduates",
         mean = comma(mean, accuracy = .01),
         sd = comma(sd, accuracy = .01))

cte.n.courses.summary.ctestudents <- master.4 %>%
  filter(total.cte.courses.taken > 0) %>%
  summarise(mean = mean(total.cte.courses.taken),
            median = median(total.cte.courses.taken),
            sd = sd(total.cte.courses.taken),
            n = comma(n(), accuracy = 1),
            min = min(total.cte.courses.taken),
            max = max(total.cte.courses.taken)) %>%
  mutate(population = "Only graduates with CTE courses > 0",
         mean = comma(mean, accuracy = .01),
         sd = comma(sd, accuracy = .01))
  
cte.n.courses.summary.total.ctestudents <- cte.n.courses.summary.total %>%
  rbind(cte.n.courses.summary.ctestudents) %>%
  select(population, n, mean, median, sd, min, max)

datatable(cte.n.courses.summary.total.ctestudents, class = "cell-border stripe", filter = "top")






Below is a chart showing the distribution of CTE courses taken by individuals. This shows that a a large majority of students take 5 courses or less.


master.4.hist <- master.4 %>%
  mutate(key = seq(n())) %>%
  select(key, total.cte.courses.taken)

cte.n.courses.taken.dist.plot <- ggplot(master.4.hist, aes(total.cte.courses.taken)) +
  geom_histogram_interactive(aes(data_id = key, tooltip = paste("N = ", comma(..count.., accuracy = 1), "\nPercent: ", percent(..count.. / sum(..count..), accuracy = .1)))) +
  labs(x="", y = "", color="", title = "Histogram - N CTE courses")+
  scale_y_continuous(labels=scales::comma)+
  theme_line+
  theme(legend.position = "bottom",
        text = element_text(size = 16))

  girafe(ggobj = cte.n.courses.taken.dist.plot, width_svg = 10) %>%
    girafe_options(opts_selection(type = "none"),
                   opts_toolbar(saveaspng = FALSE),
                   opts_sizing(rescale = FALSE))






The following table shows that nearly three-quarters of the students took at least one CTE course.


cte.pct <- master.4 %>%
  mutate(took.CTE = ifelse(total.cte.courses.taken > 0, "Yes", "No")) %>%
  group_by(took.CTE) %>%
  summarize(n = n()) %>%
  ungroup()  %>%
  mutate(pct = n / sum(n))

datatable(cte.pct, class = "cell-border stripe", filter = "top", rownames = FALSE,
          options = list(columnDefs = list(list(className = "dt-center", targets = 1)))) %>%
  formatCurrency(2, "", digits = 0) %>%
  formatPercentage(3, digits = 1)






Up next is to see if the percentage of students taking a CTE course varies significantly by RUCA group.
There is a significant difference in whether a student has taken at least one CTE course and their high school county RUCA category. Although 72% of all graduates took at least one CTE course, that percentage is highest in more rural districts. 85.7% took at least one CTE course in entirely rural districts while 80.2% took at least one in town/rural mix districts. 67.5% took at least one in our urban/town/rural mix districts.
Of those students that took at least 1 CTE course, the average number of CTE courses taken ranged from 3.7 in our entirely rural districts to 3.1 in urban/town/rural mix districts.

title: CTEEnrollment
section: Summary - CareerCluster of CTE courses taken
text:
Summary - CareerCluster of CTE courses taken
Let’s dig into the breadth of CTE course concentrations a graduate would take by looking at the proportion of graduates that took at least one course within a concentration.
The table below shows that nearly a third of all graduates took a CTE course in Transportation, Distribution & Logistics, followed by 20% in Manufacturing, and 16% in each Architecture & Construction and Human Services.


cte.cf.prop <- master.4 %>%
  gather(key = "CareerCluster", value = "n.courses", `ACTE-SPED`:`Youth Apprenticeship`) %>%
  mutate(cte.cf.taken = ifelse(n.courses > 0, "Yes", "No")) %>%
  tabyl(CareerCluster, cte.cf.taken) %>%
  mutate(pct.taken.cf = Yes / (Yes + No)) %>% 
  arrange(desc(pct.taken.cf))

datatable(cte.cf.prop, class = "cell-border stripe", filter = "top", rownames = FALSE,
          options = list(scrollX = TRUE)) %>%
  formatCurrency(2:3, "", digits = 0) %>%
  formatPercentage(4)






Now we will take a look at the breakdown of the number of times a CTE courses has been taken within a CareerCluster for each PersonID. I expect there to be a lot of variation in this data since different schools might focus on different types of CTE offerings depending on the local employment makeup.
First, lets look at the concentrations of courses taken across CareerClusters.
Not surprisingly, Transportation, Distribution & Logistics was the careercluster with the highest percentage of courses taken with 19.6%. This was followed by manufacturing with 12.4% and architecture and construction with 11.0% of CTE courses taken in that CareerCluster.


cte.cf.concentration.total <- master.4 %>%
  select(PersonID,  `ACTE-SPED`:`Youth Apprenticeship`) %>%
  gather(key = "CareerCluster", value = "n.courses", 2:ncol(.)) %>%
  group_by(CareerCluster) %>%
  summarise(n = sum(n.courses)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(pct = percent(n / sum(n), accuracy = .1)) %>%
  arrange(CareerCluster)

  datatable(cte.cf.concentration.total, class = "cell-border stripe", filter = "top", rownames = FALSE)






Lets see how this looks broken down by county.
The county maps do show some differences in percentages across career clusters. Manufacturing was consistently offered and taken across the region, as well as transportation, distribution and logistics and Human Services.
Koochiching has a high percentage of students that take health science & health occupations as well as human services.


cte.cf.concentration.county <- master.4 %>%
  select(PersonID, county.name, countyfp,  `ACTE-SPED`:`Youth Apprenticeship`) %>%
  gather(key = "CareerCluster", value = "n.courses",  `ACTE-SPED`:`Youth Apprenticeship`) %>%
  group_by(county.name, countyfp, CareerCluster) %>%
  summarise(n = sum(n.courses)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  group_by(county.name, countyfp) %>%
  mutate(pct = n / sum(n)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  rename(CareerClusterName = CareerCluster) %>%
  left_join(mn_counties[,c(5,7)], by = "countyfp")

cte.cf.concentration.county.map <- ggplot(data = filter(cte.cf.concentration.county, pct > .05)) +
  facet_wrap(~CareerClusterName, ncol = 2,
             labeller = label_wrap_gen(15)) +
  geom_sf_interactive(color = "grey85", aes(geometry = geometry, fill = pct, data_id = countyfp, tooltip = paste(county.name, "\nCareerCluster: ", CareerClusterName, "\nPercent of courses taken in this CareerCluster: ", percent(pct, accuracy = .1), sep = ""))) +
  theme_sf+
  scale_fill_fermenter(palette = "PuBu", direction = 1, labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(title = str_wrap("Percent of CTE courses taken within each CareerCluster by county", 39)) +
  theme(legend.box.margin = margin(0, 0, 0, 0),
        text = element_text(size = 16),
        strip.text = element_text(size = 8))

girafe(ggobj = cte.cf.concentration.county.map, height_svg = 20) %>%
  girafe_options(opts_sizing(rescale = FALSE))






The next big question is whether these percentages vary by year. Are there any trends?
This is honestly a bit surprising. The chart raises a couple of questions.
There was a big increase in the transportation, distribution and logistics career cluster in the mid-2010s but has declined substantially since that time. Health science and health occupations has been growing steadily as well as architecture and construction.


cte.cf.concentration.year <- master.4 %>%
  select(PersonID, grad.year, `ACTE-SPED`:`Youth Apprenticeship`) %>%
  gather(key = "CareerCluster", value = "n.courses", `ACTE-SPED`:`Youth Apprenticeship`) %>%
  group_by(grad.year, CareerCluster) %>%
  summarise(n = sum(n.courses)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  group_by(grad.year) %>%
  mutate(pct = n / sum(n)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  filter(grad.year > 2006) %>%
  mutate(data_id = seq(n())) %>%
  rename(CareerClusterName = CareerCluster) 


cte.cf.concentration.year.plot <- ggplot(cte.cf.concentration.year, aes(grad.year, pct, color = CareerClusterName)) +
  geom_point_interactive(size = 3, aes(data_id = data_id, tooltip = paste(CareerClusterName, "\nYear: ", grad.year, "\nCareerCluster: ", CareerClusterName, "\nPercent of CTE courses taken: ", percent(pct, accuracy = .1), sep = ""))) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(x="", y = "", color="", title = "Percent of taken CTE courses")+
  geom_label(data = filter(cte.cf.concentration.year, grad.year == max(cte.cf.concentration.year$grad.year)), aes(label = percent(pct, accuracy = .1)), show.legend = FALSE, size = 5) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels=scales::percent)+
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1900, 2050, 2),
                     guide = guide_axis(n.dodge = 2)) +
  theme_line+
  scale_color_discrete(guide = guide_legend(ncol = 3)) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom",
        text = element_text(size = 14))

  girafe(ggobj = cte.cf.concentration.year.plot, width_svg = 10, height_svg = 7) %>%
    girafe_options(opts_selection(type = "none"),
                   opts_toolbar(saveaspng = FALSE),
                   opts_sizing(rescale = FALSE))







write_csv(master.4, "Data/SLEDS/Masters/Master-4.csv")

We have 5,744,192 rows and 5 columns in this dataset. Here are the descriptions for each of the columns.

K12AsstTimeID: Day, month, and year the assessment took place.
TestName: Name of the test taken. There are 12 different tests in the dataset -

ACCESS: English proficiency,
ALTACCESS: English proficiency for special education or meet requirements
MCA-II & MCA-III: Minnesota Comprehsensive Assessments (series 2 and 3)
MOD-II, MOD-III: Modified Comprehensive Assessment, used only until 2014
MTAS & MTAS-III: Minnesota Test of Academic Skills
MTELL: an alternate assessment for students learning English (like the MTAS or MOD). MTELL was only administered from 2007-2010 during the series-II of MCAs.
SOLOM: Minnesota Student Oral Language Observation Matrix
TEAE: one of two assessments that Minnesota used to meet the requirements to test ELs in all four domains of language (the other was SOLOM). TEAE was used 2002 until we changed to ACCESS in 2012. SOLOM was used 2004 until we changed to ACCESS in 2012.

Subject: Classifies each test that is given to a student based on the areas measured. There are 8 factors;

A: Aural (listening) - ACCESS & ALTACCESS only
C: Composite - ACCESS & ALTACCESS only
L: Listening/Speaking
M: Math
O: Oral - ACCESS & ALTACCESS only
R: Reading
S: Science
W: Writing

GradeTested: Grade student was enrolled in when performing assessment.
AchievementLevel: Used to count the number of students in each achievement level by group such as race, gender, and ethnicity. It must be calculated from other students at a similar graden and subject for a specific year.

ACCESS students are graded on a language proficiency scale of 1 through 6.
ALT-ACCESS students are graded using a P1 through P3 and A1 through A3 scale.
There are 4 different levels for the MCA test

D: Does not meet standards
E: Exceeds standards
M: Meets Standards
P: Partially meets standards

SOLOM tests are 1-5 scale with 5 being the highest
TEAE tests are 1-5 scale with 5 being the highest.


There are two ways in which we are going to code our graduates.
The first is to identify whether a student has been identified as an English learner. This means filtering students that have taken the ACCESS, ALT-ACCESS, MTELL, MTAS, TEAE, MOD-II, MOD-III, or SOLOM at least once in their career.
The second is be determining their highest achievement level in each subject of the MCA tests within the dataset. The dataset provides each instance of a test for each student so many are students are listed numerous times - once for each time they took a test.
Lets do this in two separate files and then join each with the master file.
Starting with identifying the EL students.


el <- assessments.original %>%
  filter(!TestName %in% c("MCA-II", "MCA-III")) %>%
  distinct(PersonID, .keep_all = TRUE) %>%
  select(PersonID) %>%
  mutate(english.learner = 1)

This dataset identified 34,995 individuals who were identified as an english learner at least one time in the original dataset.
Now we will determine the highest achievement level for each subject for each student.


mca <- assessments.original %>%
  filter(TestName %in% c("MCA-II", "MCA-III")) %>%
  filter(AchievementLevel != "NULL") %>%
  droplevels() %>%
  mutate(AchievementLevelCode = ifelse(AchievementLevel == "D", 1,
                                       ifelse(AchievementLevel == "P", 2,
                                              ifelse(AchievementLevel == "M", 3, 4))))

mca.highest <- mca %>%
  group_by(PersonID, Subject) %>%
  filter(AchievementLevelCode == max(AchievementLevelCode)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  select(PersonID, Subject, AchievementLevelCode) %>%
  mutate(mca.subject = paste("MCA.", Subject, sep = "")) %>%
  select(PersonID, mca.subject, AchievementLevelCode) %>%
  mutate(id = seq(n())) %>%
  spread(key = mca.subject, value = AchievementLevelCode) %>%
  group_by(PersonID) %>%
  fill(MCA.M, .direction = c("downup")) %>%
  fill(MCA.R, .direction = "downup") %>%
  fill(MCA.S, .direction = "downup") %>%
  distinct(PersonID, .keep_all = TRUE) %>%
  select(-id)

  mutate(PersonID = as.integer(PersonID)) %>%
  left_join(el, by = "PersonID") %>%
  left_join(mca.highest, by = "PersonID") %>%
  mutate(english.learner = ifelse(is.na(english.learner), 0, english.learner))

Summary of SAT data
Lets check to see what percentage of the master dataset has taken the SAT.
There is a tiny percentage of the dataset that has taken the SAT, 1.7%. With this information I don’t see a need to check whether there is a significant difference in students taking the SAT based on RUCA category or County. Even if there is a significant difference, there just isn’t enough observations to make a difference.


sat.total <- master.8 %>%
  group_by(sat.taken) %>%
  summarize(n = n()) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(pct = n / sum(n))

datatable(sat.total, class = "cell-border stripe", filter = "top", rownames = FALSE,
          options = list(columnDefs = list(list(className = "dt-center", targets = 0:1))))  %>%
  formatPercentage(3, digits = 1) %>%
  formatCurrency(2, digits = 0, "")

title: Categorizing Range Schools
section: Primary Iron Range School Districts (Core Iron Range)
text:
Primary Iron Range School Districts (Core Iron Range)
These are located directly within the Mesabi Iron Range and are almost always considered part of it:

Rock Ridge Public Schools (ISD 2909) – Formed by the merger of Virginia and Eveleth-Gilbert district
Mountain Iron-Buhl (ISD 712)
Chisholm (ISD 695)
Hibbing (ISD 701)
Nashwauk-Keewatin (ISD 319)
Ely (ISD 696)
Mesabi East (ISD 2711) – Based in Aurora, serving Aurora, Hoyt Lakes, and Biwabik.

title: Categorizing Range Schools
section: Borderline or Secondary Iron Range School Districts
text:
Borderline or Secondary Iron Range School Districts
These districts are near the Iron Range and are sometimes included depending on the context:

Cook County (ISD 166) – More North Shore than Iron Range, but very rural and sometimes lumped into broader regional definitions.
Northland Community Schools (ISD 118, in Remer) – Not on the Mesabi Range, but sometimes included in broader northeastern discussions.
Floodwood (ISD 698) – Located west of Duluth and near the southern edge of Iron Range influence.

Deer River (ISD 317) – South and west of Grand Rapids; sometimes considered part of the western fringe.
Grand Rapids (ISD 318) – A larger hub district west of the traditional range; sometimes included as a key service and economic center for the region.

title: Categorizing Range Schools
text:
Not Typically Considered Iron Range
These are nearby but not part of the Iron Range proper:

Duluth Public Schools (ISD 709) – Major city in NE MN, but culturally and economically separate from the Iron Range.
Two Harbors/Silver Bay (Lake Superior ISD 381) – On the North Shore.
Carlton, Cloquet, Moose Lake – More in the Carlton County area, not considered Iron Range.
International Falls (ISD 361) – Farther north, part of the borderlands, not the Range.

In the original dataset we have 1598552 rows and 16 columns. Below is a description of each variable.

Empl_TimeID: Last day of fiscal quarter
CalendarYear: Year
CalendarQuarter: Quarter within the year in which the data applies. Quarters are;

1 = Jan - Mar
2 = Apr - Jun
3 = Jul - Sep
4 = Oct - Dec

EmploymentOrganizationID: An internal identification for each employer.
EmployeeQuarterlyHoursWorked: The total number of hours worked by an employee at an employer’s location during a specific calendar quarter
EmployeeQuarterlyWages: The total wages earned by an employee at an employer’s location during a specific calendar quarter
EmployeeTenure: The total number of quarters a worker has been employeed by an organization at a specific location, up to an including the current calendar quarter
IndustryID: Auto generated ID code for a record in the Industry dimension.
USIndustryCode: Six-digit North American Industrial Classification System (NAICS) code
GroupCode: Four-digit North American Industrial Classification System (NAICS) code
IndustryGroup: Definition of GroupCode variable, the 4-digit NAICS code
OwnershipCode: A classification system based upon the controlling interest of the establishment primarily designed to distinguish between governmental and non-governmental establishments

10 = Federal government
20 = State government
30 = Local government
50 = Private

EmployerLocationTotalWagesPaid: The total wages paid to all workers employeed by an organization at a specific location during a specific calendar quarter
QuarterlyAverageEmployment: The average number of workers employeed by an organization at a specific location during a specific calendar quarter
LocationID: ???
EconomicDevelopmentRegion: The 13 economic development regions within the state of Minnesota as defined by the Department of Employment and Economic Development (DEED).

R01000 EDR 1 - Northwest

R02000 EDR 2 - Headwaters

R03000 EDR 3 - Arrowhead

R04000 EDR 4 - West Central

R05000 EDR 5 - North Central

R06E00 EDR 6E - Southwest Central

R06W00 EDR 6W - Upper Minnesota Valley

R07E00 EDR 7E - East Central

R07W00 EDR 7W - Central

R08000 EDR 8 - Southwest

R09000 EDR 9 - South Central

R10000 EDR 10 - Southeast
R11000 EDR 11 - 7 County Twin Cities

EconomicDevelopmentRegionName: Name of EDR
County: Minnesota county code to which this institution belongs. This can be used as a foreign key into the Geography dimension on MNCounty.

Link to codes

CountyName: The name of the county corresponding to the County and MNCounty Codes for this Location.
MNCounty: County Code for this location as assigned by the state of Minnesota.

Link to codes City: All of the city data is NA



So all the previous datasets we structured and filtered so that each observation in the master dataset was an individual. We will want to continue to do the same. So we need to create an employment dataset with the following columns;

PersonID
High school graduation year
Whether the individual had an employment record the year of, and each subsequent year, of high school graduation.
How many years after graduation each employment check is (i.e. grad.year.1, grad.year.2,….etc.)





grad.years <- read_csv("Data/SLEDS/Masters/Master-10.csv") %>%
  select(PersonID, hs.grad.year)

mn.emp.record.year <- employment.original %>%
  mutate(CalendarYear = as.integer(str_sub(TimeID, 1, 4))) %>%
  select(PersonID, CalendarYear) %>%
  distinct(PersonID, CalendarYear) %>%
  mutate(mn.emp.record = "MN emp record") %>%
  filter(CalendarYear > 2007) %>%
  filter(CalendarYear < 2024) %>%
  complete(PersonID, CalendarYear, fill = list(mn.emp.record = "No MN emp record")) 

mn.emp.record <- grad.years %>%
  left_join(mn.emp.record.year, by = c("PersonID")) %>%
  mutate(CalendarYear = ifelse(is.na(CalendarYear), hs.grad.year, CalendarYear),
         mn.emp.record = ifelse(is.na(mn.emp.record), "No MN emp record", mn.emp.record),
         update = ifelse(CalendarYear < hs.grad.year, "Not graduated HS", "Graduated")) %>%
  filter(update == "Graduated") %>%
  select(-update) %>%
  group_by(PersonID) %>%
  mutate(grad.year.seq = seq(n())) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  complete(PersonID, grad.year.seq) %>%
  group_by(PersonID) %>%
  fill(hs.grad.year, .direction = "down") %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(CalendarYear = ifelse(is.na(CalendarYear), hs.grad.year + (grad.year.seq - 1), CalendarYear),
         mn.emp.record = ifelse(CalendarYear > 2023, "After 2023", mn.emp.record),
         mn.emp.record = ifelse(is.na(mn.emp.record), "No MN emp record", mn.emp.record),
         grad.year = paste("grad.year.", grad.year.seq-1, sep = "")) %>%
  select(-grad.year.seq)

The dataset above provides each unique PersonID from our master list along with each possible grad year and subsequent years (grad.year.0, grad.year.1, grad.year.2 … grad.year.11).
Here is the logic;

grad.year.x > 2023: mn.emp.record == “After 2023”,
if there’s a MN employment record for the PersonID and the grad.year.x: mn.emp.record == “MN emp record”
if there’s no MN employment record for the PersonID and the grad.year.x: mn.emp.record == “No MN emp record”

There are 797,056 rows in this dataset with 49,816 individuals.




The biggest issue is how do we get a meaningful indicator on whether they were employed in the region and whether they are employed in an industry that matches their CTE experience that wasn’t just a “summer job”. We need to filter out summer jobs between college years, as well as adapt to different paths that students take.
We will define “meaningful employment” as an employment experience in which an individual works for one particular employer for 1,000 hours worked in any given year.
This will be a couple step process. First we will build a dataset that has each grad.year.x from each PersonID high school graduation year and match it with the MN employment records. We will end up with each PersonID having each grad.year.x along with wither they have a MN employment record, whether they had meaningful employment, whether grad.year.x is after 2019, or whether they have no MN employment record.


meaningful.employer <- employment.original %>%
  mutate(CalendarYear = as.integer(str_sub(TimeID, 1, 4))) %>%
  group_by(PersonID, EmploymentOrganizationID, CalendarYear) %>%
  summarize(AnnualHoursWorked = sum(EmployeeQuarterlyHoursWorked)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  group_by(PersonID) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  right_join(mn.emp.record, by = c("PersonID", "CalendarYear")) %>%
  mutate(grad.year = fct_relevel(grad.year, "grad.year.0", "grad.year.1", "grad.year.2", "grad.year.3", "grad.year.4", "grad.year.5", "grad.year.6", "grad.year.7", "grad.year.8", "grad.year.9", "grad.year.10", "grad.year.11"),
         new.mn.emp.record = ifelse(AnnualHoursWorked > 999, "Meaningful employment", mn.emp.record),
         new.mn.emp.record = ifelse(CalendarYear > 2023, "After 2023", new.mn.emp.record),
         new.mn.emp.record = ifelse(new.mn.emp.record == "MN emp record", "MN emp record - not meaningful", new.mn.emp.record),
         new.mn.emp.record = ifelse(mn.emp.record == "No MN emp record", "No MN emp record", new.mn.emp.record),
         meaningful.emp.code = ifelse(new.mn.emp.record == "Meaningful employment", 1, 0)) %>%
  group_by(PersonID, CalendarYear) %>%
  filter(meaningful.emp.code == max(meaningful.emp.code)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  distinct(PersonID, grad.year, meaningful.emp.code, .keep_all = TRUE)

Now, we want to determine if the locations of meaningful employment match the counties and regions from which they graduated high school. To do this, we will import the latest master dataset so we can compare their high school locations with meaningful employment locations.


emp.original.locations <- employment.original %>%
  mutate(CalendarYear = as.integer(str_sub(TimeID, 1, 4)),
         CountyName = str_replace(CountyName, " County", ""),
         CountyName = str_replace(CountyName, "Saint Louis", "St. Louis"),
         CountyName = str_replace(CountyName, "City of Duluth", "St. Louis"),
         CountyName = str_replace(CountyName, "City of Minneapolis", "Hennepin"),
         CountyName = str_replace(CountyName, "City of St. Paul", "Ramsey"),
         CountyName = str_replace(CountyName, "Shakopee Mdewakanton Community", "Scott"),
         CountyName = str_replace(CountyName, "White Earth Tribal Counci", "Mahnomen")) %>%
  left_join(counties.regions.1, by = c("CountyName" = "Name")) %>%
  rename(EconomicDevelopmentRegionName = edr) %>%
  select(PersonID, CalendarYear, EmploymentOrganizationID, EconomicDevelopmentRegionName, CountyName, project.pr) %>%
  distinct(PersonID, CalendarYear, EmploymentOrganizationID, EconomicDevelopmentRegionName, CountyName, project.pr) %>%
  rename(employment.county = CountyName,
         emp.edr = EconomicDevelopmentRegionName,
         emp.pr = project.pr) %>%
  mutate(emp.edr = str_replace(emp.edr, "  ", " "),
         emp.edr = as.factor(emp.edr),
         employment.county = str_replace(employment.county, " County", ""),
         employment.county = str_replace(employment.county, "City of Duluth", "St. Louis"),
         employment.county = str_replace(employment.county, "Saint Louis", "St. Louis"),
         employment.county = str_replace(employment.county, "City of Minneapolis", "Hennepin"),
         employment.county = str_replace(employment.county, "City of St. Paul", "Ramsey"),
         employment.county = str_replace(employment.county, "White Earth Tribal Counci", "Mahnomen"),
         employment.county = as.factor(employment.county)) %>%
  left_join(counties.regions[,c(2,4)], by = c("employment.county" = "Name")) %>%
  rename(emp.Dem_Desc = Dem_Desc) 

meaningful.emp.locations <- meaningful.employer %>%
  left_join(emp.original.locations, by = c("PersonID", "CalendarYear", "EmploymentOrganizationID")) %>%
  mutate(emp.edr = ifelse(employment.county == "Statewide (i.e. no fixed location)", "Unknown", as.character(emp.edr)),
         emp.Dem_Desc = ifelse(employment.county == "Statewide (i.e. no fixed location)", "Unknown", as.character(emp.Dem_Desc)),
         emp.edr = ifelse(employment.county == "Hennepin", "EDR 11 - 7 County Twin Cities", emp.edr),
         emp.edr = ifelse(employment.county == "Ramsey", "EDR 11 - 7 County Twin Cities", emp.edr),
         emp.edr = ifelse(employment.county == "St. Louis", "EDR 3 - Arrowhead", emp.edr),
         emp.edr = ifelse(employment.county == "Unknown", "Unknown", emp.edr),
         emp.Dem_Desc = ifelse(employment.county == "Unknown", "Unknown", as.character(emp.Dem_Desc)),
         emp.Dem_Desc = ifelse(employment.county == "NULL", "NULL", as.character(emp.Dem_Desc)),
         emp.edr = ifelse(employment.county == "Mahnomen", "EDR 2 - Headwaters", emp.edr))

grad.locations <- read_csv("Data/SLEDS/Masters/Master-10.csv") %>%
  select(PersonID, county.name, Dem_Desc, edr) %>%
  rename(hs.county.name = county.name,
         hs.Dem_Desc = Dem_Desc,
         hs.edr = edr)

grad.emp.location.match <- grad.locations %>%
  right_join(meaningful.emp.locations, by = "PersonID") %>%
  mutate(county.match = new.mn.emp.record,
         new.county.match = ifelse(county.match == "Meaningful employment" & employment.county == hs.county.name, "Meaningful emp - match", county.match),
         new.county.match = ifelse(new.county.match == "Meaningful employment", "Meaningful emp - no match", new.county.match),
         new.county.match = fct_relevel(new.county.match, "Meaningful emp - match", "Meaningful emp - no match", "MN emp record - not meaningful", "No MN emp record", "After 2023")) %>%
  select(-county.match) %>%
  rename(county.match = new.county.match) %>%
  mutate(edr.match = new.mn.emp.record,
         new.edr.match = ifelse(edr.match == "Meaningful employment" & emp.edr == hs.edr, "Meaningful emp - match", edr.match),
         new.edr.match = ifelse(new.edr.match == "Meaningful employment", "Meaningful emp - no match", new.edr.match),
         new.edr.match = fct_relevel(new.edr.match, "Meaningful emp - match", "Meaningful emp - no match", "MN emp record - not meaningful", "No MN emp record", "After 2023")) %>%
  select(-edr.match) %>%
  rename(edr.match = new.edr.match) %>%
  mutate(region.match = new.mn.emp.record,
         new.region.match = ifelse(region.match == "Meaningful employment" & emp.pr %in% c("Northeast"), "Meaningful emp - match", region.match),
         new.region.match = ifelse(new.region.match == "Meaningful employment", "Meaningful emp - no match", new.region.match),
         new.region.match = fct_relevel(new.region.match, "Meaningful emp - match", "Meaningful emp - no match", "MN emp record - not meaningful", "No MN emp record", "After 2023")) %>%
  select(-region.match) %>%
  rename(region.match = new.region.match) %>%
  mutate(state.match = new.mn.emp.record,
         new.state.match = ifelse(!is.na(emp.edr) & state.match == "Meaningful employment", "Meaningful emp - match",
                                  ifelse(employment.county == "Statewide (i.e. no fixed location)" & state.match == "Meaningful employment", "Meaningful emp - match", state.match)),
         new.state.match = fct_relevel(new.state.match, "Meaningful emp - match", "MN emp record - not meaningful", "No MN emp record", "After 2023")) %>%
  select(-state.match) %>%
  rename(state.match = new.state.match) %>%
  mutate(Dem_Desc.match = new.mn.emp.record,

  mutate(CalendarYear = ifelse(is.na(CalendarYear), hs.grad.year + (grad.year.seq - 1), CalendarYear),
         mn.emp.record = ifelse(CalendarYear > 2023, "After 2023", mn.emp.record),
         mn.emp.record = ifelse(is.na(mn.emp.record), "No MN emp record", mn.emp.record),
