My goal is to end up with a dataset where each observation (row) represents a unique (unduplicated) individual that’s tied to the school from which they graduated. Here’s how I will do that.

PersonID: change to integer
K12OrganizationID: change to integer.
K12EnrTimeID: Change so it’s only the year
Grade: eliminate - unimportant since we are mostly concerned about whether they graduated.
EconomicStatusIndicator: I will change this to two categories. Whether they were ever eligible for reduce priced or free meal will be coded as 1 (eligible = codes 1, 2, 4, 5) at any point in the dataset. The remaining will be coded as 0.
FederalRaceIndicator: eliminate - I’m going to use the RaceEthnicity column instead.
PSEO columns: I’m most concerned about whether they participated in PSEO or not. A new column will be created indicated whether there was a “Y” coded for either the “PSEOConcurrentEnrollmentIndicator” or “PostSecondaryEnrollmentOptionsIndicator” columns at any point in the dataset. The two original columns will be eliminated.
StatusEnd: I will only include individuals that have StatusEnd coded as an 8 or 9.
Gender: included and not changed.
SpecialEdStatus: I will split this into two categories. The first is that a student did not require special education services (codes 1-2) at any point in the dataset. The other category will be that they require special education (codes 4 - 9) at any point in the dataset.
Limited English: keep with no changes.
Primary language: I’m going to create two categories. One being that English is the primary language while the other will be that English is NOT the primary language at any point in the dataset.
Homeless: Keep with no changes.

We first need to create a list of all individuals with the StatusEnd code of 8 or 9 (graduated). In addition, we need to remove any student that graduated before 2008. This is because we will not have their full Sophmore - Senior records which is especially important when attempting to identify whether the number of CTE courses taken predicts migration.
The other element I want to add is a pre-covid and post-covid variable. All individuals whose grad year is before 2020 will be labeled pre-covid and all others wil lbe post-covid.
This “graduates list” will be the list on which we will bind all the other variables.


graduates <- enrollment.org.ne %>%
  filter(StatusEnd %in% c(8,9)) %>%
  mutate(grad.year = str_sub(TimeID, 1, 4),
         grad.year = as.integer(grad.year),
         grad.year.covid = ifelse(grad.year > 2019, "Post-covid grad", "Pre-covid grad")) %>%
  select(PersonID, K12OrganizationID, OrganizationName, grad.year, grad.year.covid, Gender, LimitedEnglishProficiencyIndicator, HomelessIndicator, county.name, countyfp, Dem_Desc, edr, planning.region) %>%
  distinct(PersonID, .keep_all = TRUE) %>%
  filter(grad.year > 2007) 


Next we need to create new columns for the variables that will indicate a certain status has been met at any point in the dataset for each PersonID. For example, we want a column that indicates a PersonID was enrolled in PSEO at some point in the dataset. The variables that need a new column created are;

EconomicStatusIndicator
PostSecondaryEnrollmentOptionsIndicator & PSEOConcurrentEnrollmentIndicator
SpecialEdStatus
HomeprimaryLanguage



# Lets start with economic status indicator
k12.enr.esi.indicator <- enrollment.org.ne %>%
  select(PersonID, EconomicStatusIndicator) %>%
  group_by(PersonID) %>%
  mutate(economic.status.code = ifelse(EconomicStatusIndicator %in% c(1,2,4,5), 1, 0),
         economic.status.code.sum = sum(economic.status.code)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  distinct(PersonID, .keep_all = TRUE) %>%
  mutate(economic.status = ifelse(economic.status.code.sum > 0, 1, 0)) %>%
  select(PersonID, economic.status)

# PSEO

k12.enr.pseo.indicator <- enrollment.org.ne%>%
  select(PersonID, PostSecondaryEnrollmentOptionsIndicator, PSEOConcurrentEnrollmentIndicator) %>%
  mutate(PostSecondaryEnrollmentOptionsIndicator = ifelse(PostSecondaryEnrollmentOptionsIndicator == "Y", 1, 0),
         PSEOConcurrentEnrollmentIndicator = ifelse(PSEOConcurrentEnrollmentIndicator == "Y", 1, 0)) %>%
  gather(key = "pseo.type", value = "indicator", 2:3) %>%
  group_by(PersonID) %>%
  summarise(pseo = sum(indicator)) %>%
  mutate(pseo.participant = ifelse(pseo > 0, 1, 0)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  select(PersonID, pseo.participant)

# Special Ed status

k12.enr.spced.indicator <- enrollment.org.ne %>%
  select(PersonID, SpecialEdStatus) %>%
  mutate(SpecialEdStatus.code = ifelse(SpecialEdStatus %in% c(4,5,6,7,8,9), 1, 0)) %>%
  group_by(PersonID) %>%
  summarise(SpecialEdStatus.sum = sum(SpecialEdStatus.code)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(SpecialEdStatus = ifelse(SpecialEdStatus.sum > 0, 1, 0)) %>%
  select(PersonID, SpecialEdStatus)

# Home Primary Language

k12.enr.homeprimlang.indicator <- enrollment.org.ne %>%
  select(PersonID, HomePrimaryLanguage) %>%
  mutate(HomePrimaryLanguage.code = ifelse(HomePrimaryLanguage == 11, 0, 1)) %>%
  group_by(PersonID) %>%
  summarise(HomePrimaryLanguage.sum = sum(HomePrimaryLanguage.code)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(non.english.home = ifelse(HomePrimaryLanguage.sum > 0, 1, 0)) %>%
  select(PersonID, non.english.home)

# Race

k12.enr.race <- enrollment.org.ne %>%
  select(PersonID, RaceEthnicity) %>%
  mutate(RaceEthnicity = ifelse(RaceEthnicity == 0, "Unknown",
                                ifelse(RaceEthnicity == 1, "AI",
                                       ifelse(RaceEthnicity == 2, "Asian/PI",
                                              ifelse(RaceEthnicity == 3, "Hispanic",
                                                     ifelse(RaceEthnicity == 4, "Black", "White"))))),
         RaceEthnicity = as.factor(RaceEthnicity)) %>%
  distinct(PersonID, RaceEthnicity) %>%
  mutate(code = ifelse(RaceEthnicity == "Unknown", 0, 1)) %>%
  group_by(PersonID) %>%
  filter(code == max(code)) %>%
  ungroup %>%
  distinct(PersonID, .keep_all = TRUE) %>%
  select(PersonID, RaceEthnicity)


Now we can combine the list of graduates with the status indicators.


k12.enrollment.master <- graduates %>%
  left_join(k12.enr.esi.indicator, by = "PersonID") %>%
  left_join(k12.enr.pseo.indicator, by = "PersonID") %>%
  left_join(k12.enr.spced.indicator, by = "PersonID") %>%
  left_join(k12.enr.homeprimlang.indicator, by = "PersonID") %>%
  left_join(k12.enr.race, by = "PersonID") %>%
  select(PersonID, K12OrganizationID, OrganizationName, county.name, countyfp, Dem_Desc, edr, planning.region, grad.year, grad.year.covid, Gender, LimitedEnglishProficiencyIndicator, HomelessIndicator, economic.status, pseo.participant, SpecialEdStatus, non.english.home, RaceEthnicity)

title: Post-secondary pathways
text:
Key Findings

Demographics are the strongest and most consistent predictors across all three outcomes.

Economic Status: Economically disadvantaged students lagged behind at every stage—less likely to enroll immediately, less likely to attend at all, and much less likely to graduate.
Race/Ethnicity: White and Asian/PI students consistently had higher enrollment and graduation rates, while American Indian, Black, and Hispanic students faced persistent barriers at all stages, with the largest disparities at completion.
Special Education Status: Students with special education status showed markedly lower rates of enrollment, attendance, and especially graduation.

High School Characteristics showed weak associations.

School Locale: Rural, mixed, and urban settings had minimal differences in postsecondary pathways.
Community Economic Conditions: Students from lower-unemployment, higher-wage areas were modestly more likely to enroll, attend, and graduate, but these effects were smaller than individual-level demographics or accomplishments.

High School Accomplishments were powerful predictors, especially for enrollment and graduation.

Academic Achievement: ACT and MCA scores (particularly Reading and Science) were strongly linked to both immediate enrollment and graduation, showing that academic readiness is a key driver of persistence and attainment.
PSEO Participation: The single strongest programmatic predictor across all outcomes. PSEO students were much more likely to enroll immediately, attend at all, and eventually graduate.
CTE Involvement: Higher CTE course-taking and concentrator/completor status were associated with lower likelihood of both enrollment and graduation, suggesting that intensive CTE pathways align more with direct workforce entry than with postsecondary progression.

title: Post-secondary pathways
text:
Overall Conclusion:
Tier 1 analysis reveals that postsecondary access and attainment are shaped by both structural inequities and academic preparation. Demographic barriers—economic disadvantage, special education status, and race/ethnicity—consistently depress outcomes at every stage. Academic readiness (ACT and MCA scores) and program participation (especially PSEO) are the most powerful positive predictors of successful transitions and completion. In contrast, CTE intensity is inversely associated with postsecondary outcomes, reflecting its alignment with alternative workforce pathways.
Together, these findings suggest that strategies to improve postsecondary success must focus on closing equity gaps, bolstering academic readiness, and expanding access to PSEO and similar dual-enrollment programs, while also balancing the role of CTE in supporting both workforce entry and potential academic progression.

title: Post-secondary pathways
text:
attended.ps.within.first.year.hsgrad

Summary
Key Findings by Variable Group
Demographics

Economic Status: Cramer’s V = 0.246. Non-disadvantaged students had much higher immediate enrollment (72.1%) than disadvantaged students (47.6%). Economic disadvantage is a major barrier to direct enrollment.

Race/Ethnicity: Cramer’s V = 0.096. White (67%) and Asian/PI (58.7%) students enrolled at higher rates, while American Indian (45.8%), Black (51.4%), and Hispanic (51.6%) students enrolled at lower rates.

Special Education Status: Cramer’s V = 0.278. Students without special education status were far more likely to enroll immediately (68.6%) than those with special education status (32.6%).

High School Characteristics

School Locale (Dem_Desc): Cramer’s V = 0.022. Very weak differences across rural, mixed, and urban contexts (all ~62%).

Average Unemployment Rate: F(2, 49813) = 302.20, p < .001. Students from higher-unemployment areas were less likely to enroll immediately.

Average Wages (as % of State Average): F(2, 49813) = 33.08, p < .001. Students from higher-wage areas were slightly more likely to attend postsecondary (immediately or later).

High School Accomplishments

ACT Composite Score: F(2, 28493) = 396.75, p < .001. Higher ACT scores strongly predicted immediate enrollment, with immediate enrollees scoring about 2 points higher than non-attendees.

PSEO Participation: Cramer’s V = 0.295. PSEO participants enrolled immediately at very high rates (76.8%) compared to non-participants (48.2%).

CTE Achievement: Cramer’s V = 0.052. CTE concentrators/completors were less likely to enroll immediately (57.9%) than participants (64.9%) or non-CTE students (65.7%).

Total CTE Courses Taken: F(2, 49813) = 301.90, p < .001. More CTE courses were associated with lower immediate enrollment.

MCA Math: F(2, 47621) = 885.58, p < .001. Immediate enrollees scored much higher (0.50 points above delayed enrollees).

MCA Reading: F(2, 47319) = 1475.87, p < .001. Immediate enrollees scored substantially higher (0.46 points above non-attendees).

MCA Science: F(2, 40378) = 1025.37, p < .001. Immediate enrollees scored much higher (0.41 points above non-attendees); no difference between delayed and non-attendees.




Relative Importance of Predictors (Ranked by Effect Size/Strength of Association):

Special Education Status (Cramer’s V = 0.278) – strong demographic predictor.
PSEO Participation (Cramer’s V = 0.295) – strongest programmatic predictor.
Economic Status (Cramer’s V = 0.246) – major structural barrier.
MCA Reading (F = 1475.87) – strongest academic achievement predictor.
MCA Science (F = 1025.37) – strong academic predictor.
MCA Math (F = 885.58) – strong academic predictor.
ACT Composite Score (F = 396.75) – important test-based predictor.
Average Unemployment Rate (F = 302.20) – moderate community context effect.
Total CTE Courses Taken (F = 301.90) – more courses linked to weaker transition.
Race/Ethnicity (Cramer’s V = 0.096) – modest but meaningful disparities.
Average Wages (F = 33.08) – small community effect.
CTE Achievement (Cramer’s V = 0.052) – weak association.
School Locale (Cramer’s V = 0.022) – negligible differences.


Conclusion:
Immediate postsecondary enrollment is shaped most strongly by student characteristics (economic status, special education status, race/ethnicity), program participation (PSEO), and academic achievement (MCA and ACT scores). Community economic conditions (unemployment and wages) also matter but to a lesser extent, while school locale and CTE achievement have minimal influence. This suggests that interventions targeting equity gaps, strengthening academic preparation, and expanding access to PSEO could have the greatest impact on improving direct transitions to postsecondary education.


Demographics
Key Findings:

Economic Status: Cramer’s V = 0.246, p < .001. Non-disadvantaged students enrolled immediately at much higher rates (72.1%) than economically disadvantaged students (47.6%). Economically disadvantaged students were more likely to never attend (46.1% vs. 24.0%).
Race/Ethnicity: Cramer’s V = 0.096, p < .001. White (67%) and Asian/PI (58.7%) students had the highest immediate enrollment. American Indian students had the lowest (45.8%), while Black (51.4%) and Hispanic (51.6%) students also enrolled at below-average rates.
Special Education Status: Cramer’s V = 0.278, p < .001. Students without special education status were much more likely to enroll immediately (68.6%) than those with special education status (32.6%). Special education students were more likely to never attend (62.2% vs. 26.7%).

Conclusion:
Demographic factors play a significant role in shaping immediate postsecondary enrollment. Economic disadvantage and special education status are linked to substantially lower rates of transition, with both groups far more likely to never enroll. Race and ethnicity also matter, with White and Asian/PI students showing stronger transitions and American Indian, Black, and Hispanic students facing greater barriers. Overall, these patterns highlight persistent equity gaps in postsecondary access immediately after high school.

Key Findings:
Chi-square = 3003.42, Cramer’s V = 0.246, p < .001. Immediate enrollment (“Yes”) was much higher among students not economically disadvantaged (72.1%) than among economically disadvantaged students (47.6%). Economically disadvantaged students were more likely to never attend postsecondary (“Did not attend ps”: 46.1% vs. 24.0%) and somewhat more likely to delay enrollment beyond the first year (“No”: 6.3% vs. 3.9%).
Conclusion:
Economic disadvantage is moderately and significantly associated with lower immediate postsecondary enrollment and higher non-enrollment. Students not economically disadvantaged transition directly to college at much higher rates, while economically disadvantaged students are more likely to delay or never attend.

title: Post-secondary pathways
text:
Attended.ps

Summary
Key Findings Across Variable Groups
Demographics

Economic Status: φ = 0.228, p < .001. Non-disadvantaged students were far more likely to attend (76%) than disadvantaged students (53.9%).
Race/Ethnicity: Cramer’s V = 0.164, p < .001. White (72.4%) and Asian/PI (65.7%) students had the highest attendance, while American Indian students (51.8%) had the lowest, with Black (57.7%) and Hispanic (58.7%) also below average.
Special Education Status: φ = 0.273, p < .001. Attendance was much higher for students without special education status (73.3%) compared to those with it (37.8%).

High School Characteristics

School Locale (Dem_Desc): Cramer’s V = 0.029, p < .001. Differences across rural, town/rural mix, and urban/town/rural mix were minimal (65–69%).
Average Unemployment Rate: F(1, 49814) = 428.40, p < .001. Students from lower-unemployment areas were more likely to attend.
Average Wages (% of State Average): F(1, 49814) = 65.84, p < .001. Attendees came from areas with slightly higher average wages.

High School Accomplishments

ACT Composite Score: F(1, 28494) = 739.92, p < .001. Attendees scored about 2 points higher than non-attendees.
PSEO Participation: φ = 0.279, p < .001. Participation strongly boosted attendance (79.8% vs. 53.3%).
CTE Achievement: Cramer’s V = 0.071, p < .001. Concentrators/completors had lower attendance (62.9%) than participants (69.6%) and students with no CTE (70.4%).
Total CTE Courses Taken: F(1, 49814) = 565.70, p < .001. Non-attendees had taken more CTE courses.
MCA Math: F(1, 47622) = 1220.58, p < .001. Attendees scored 0.35 points higher.
MCA Reading: F(1, 47320) = 2654.13, p < .001. Attendees scored 0.44 points higher, the strongest MCA predictor.
MCA Science: F(1, 40379) = 1721.96, p < .001. Attendees scored 0.39 points higher.


Overall Conclusion:
Postsecondary attendance is most strongly influenced by demographic barriers (economic disadvantage, special education status, and race/ethnicity), program participation (PSEO), and academic achievement (ACT and MCA scores, especially Reading). Community economic conditions (unemployment and wages) also play a role, though weaker, while CTE involvement shows an inverse relationship—students taking more CTE courses or reaching concentrator/completor status were less likely to attend.
Taken together, the results suggest that promoting equitable access to rigorous academics, reducing economic and special education barriers, and expanding opportunities like PSEO may be the most effective levers for improving overall postsecondary participation.

Attendance was lower among Hispanic (58.7%) and Black (57.7%) students, and lowest among American Indian students (51.8%). Students classified as “Unknown” also showed below-average rates (55.8%).
Special Education Status: φ = 0.273, p < .001. Students without special education status were far more likely to attend postsecondary (73.3%) compared to students with special education status (37.8%). Special education students were more than twice as likely to never attend (62.2% vs. 26.7%).

Conclusion:
Demographic factors are strongly associated with whether students ever attend postsecondary. Economic disadvantage and special education status present the largest barriers, while racial disparities are also significant, with American Indian, Black, and Hispanic students less likely to attend. Key Findings Across Variable Groups
Demographics

Economic Status: φ = 0.270, p < .001. Graduation was much higher among non-disadvantaged students (53.1%) compared to economically disadvantaged students (25.7%). Disadvantaged students were nearly three times as likely not to graduate.
Race/Ethnicity: Cramer’s V = 0.169, p < .001 (Unknown removed). White (49.2%) and Asian/PI (44.7%) students had the highest graduation rates, while Hispanic (31.3%), Black (21.6%), and American Indian (20.8%) students had much lower rates.
Special Education Status: φ = 0.262, p < .001. Students without special education status graduated at far higher rates (48.2%) than those with it (13.2%).

High School Characteristics

School Locale (Dem_Desc): Cramer’s V = 0.022, p < .001. Graduation rates were very similar across rural (39.2%), town/rural mix (41.6%), and urban/town/rural mix (43.2%).
Average Unemployment Rate: F(1, 44033) = 572.00, p < .001. Graduates came from areas with unemployment rates about 0.33 percentage points lower than non-graduates.
Average Wages (% of State Average): F(1, 44033) = 43.37, p < .001. Graduates came from areas with wages about 0.33 percentage points higher than non-graduates.

High School Accomplishments

ACT Composite Score: F(1, 24476) = 1619.08, p < .001. Graduates scored about 2.41 points higher than non-graduates.
PSEO Participation: φ = 0.308, p < .001. Graduation was much more common among PSEO participants (57%) than non-participants (26.7%).
CTE Achievement: Cramer’s V = 0.103, p < .001. Concentrators/completors had the lowest graduation rates (35.5%), while participants (42.7%) and non-CTE students (47.5%) graduated at higher rates.
Total CTE Courses Taken: F(1, 44033) = 693.05, p < .001. Non-graduates had taken about 0.60 more CTE courses than graduates.
MCA Math: F(1, 41955) = 1748.50, p < .001. Graduates scored 0.41 points higher than non-graduates.
MCA Reading: F(1, 41687) = 3087.39, p < .001. Graduates scored 0.47 points higher, the strongest MCA predictor.
MCA Science: F(1, 34774) = 2188.12, p < .001. Graduates scored 0.44 points higher.


Overall Conclusion:
Postsecondary graduation is shaped most strongly by student-level factors. Economic disadvantage and special education status are powerful barriers, while race and ethnicity reveal deep inequities in attainment. Among school-related experiences, PSEO participation stands out as the most influential positive predictor of graduation. Academic preparation (ACT and MCA scores, especially Reading and Science) also plays a major role. In contrast, greater CTE involvement—both in number of courses and concentrator/completor status—is linked to lower graduation rates, suggesting that heavy CTE pathways align more with workforce entry than degree attainment. Community economic conditions (lower unemployment and higher wages) show modest but consistent associations.
Taken together, these findings highlight that supporting equity, strengthening academic readiness, and expanding dual-enrollment opportunities like PSEO are critical levers for increasing postsecondary completion rates.

title: Post-secondary pathways
text:
highest.cred.level

Key Findings Across Variable Groups
Demographics

Economic Status: Cramer’s V = 0.264, p < .001. Non-disadvantaged students were far more likely to earn a bachelor’s or higher (46.2% vs. 20.4%), while disadvantaged students disproportionately stopped at “Some college” (49.2% vs. 26.6%).
Race/Ethnicity: Cramer’s V = 0.088, p < .001. White (40.9%) and Asian/PI (52.5%) students had the highest bachelor’s+ attainment. Black (20.1%), Hispanic (26.7%), and American Indian (19.5%) students were far more likely to leave with “Some college” or sub-associate credentials.
Special Education Status: Cramer’s V = 0.233, p < .001. Students with special education status were overwhelmingly concentrated in “Some college” (61.6%), with very few earning a bachelor’s+ (6.9%) compared to non-special education students (41.4%).

High School Characteristics

School Locale (Dem_Desc): Cramer’s V = 0.028, p < .001. Credential attainment was nearly identical across rural, mixed, and urban/town/rural schools.
Average Unemployment Rate: F(3, 28012) = 9.11, p < .001. Students from higher-unemployment areas were slightly more likely to stop at sub-associate levels, while those from lower-unemployment areas were somewhat more likely to reach bachelor’s+.
Average Wages (% of State Average): F(3, 28012) = 6.70, p < .001. Students from higher-wage areas were modestly more likely to earn bachelor’s+, while those from lower-wage areas were slightly more likely to stop short.

High School Accomplishments

ACT Composite Score: F(3, 19493) = 1165.82, p < .001. Higher ACT scores strongly predicted bachelor’s+ attainment. “Some college” students scored similarly to associate earners, indicating persistence rather than readiness drove non-completion.
PSEO Participation: Cramer’s V = 0.308, p < .001. PSEO participants were more than twice as likely to earn a bachelor’s+ (50.5% vs. 22.2%) and much less likely to stop at “Some college.”
CTE Achievement: Cramer’s V = 0.140, p < .001. CTE concentrators/completors were more likely to stop at associate degrees (28.2%) or “Some college” (38.9%) and less likely to reach bachelor’s+ (25.6%). Non-CTE students had the highest bachelor’s+ attainment (47%).
Total CTE Courses Taken: F(3, 28012) = 471.36, p < .001. More CTE courses were associated with lower attainment; bachelor’s+ earners took the fewest CTE courses, while sub-associate and “Some college” groups took the most.
MCA Math, Reading, Science: All strongly associated with credential level (F > 850, p < .001). Bachelor’s+ earners consistently scored 0.3–0.6 points higher across subjects, with Reading and Science showing the strongest predictive value.




Overall Conclusion
The level of postsecondary credential earned is shaped most powerfully by demographic factors and academic accomplishments. Economic disadvantage, special education status, and race/ethnicity all create steep barriers, concentrating students in sub-associate outcomes or “Some college” without completion. In contrast, strong academic preparation (ACT, MCA scores) and PSEO participation sharply increase the likelihood of earning a bachelor’s or higher degree. Intensive CTE engagement, while supporting workforce readiness, is consistently associated with lower attainment levels, especially associate degrees or non-completion.
Community context (unemployment and wages) exerts a modest effect, but school locale has virtually no impact. Overall, Tier 2 results highlight that rigorous academics, equitable supports, and access to dual-enrollment opportunities are critical levers for ensuring students not only graduate but also achieve higher levels of credential attainment.



Demographics
Key Findings:

Economic Status: Cramer’s V = 0.264, p < .001. Non-disadvantaged students were far more likely to complete a bachelor’s or higher degree (46.2% vs. 20.4%) while disadvantaged students disproportionately left with “Some college” and no degree (49.2% vs. 26.6%).
Race/Ethnicity: Cramer’s V = 0.088, p < .001. White (40.9%) and Asian/PI (52.5%) students were most likely to earn bachelor’s or higher degrees, while American Indian (19.5%), Black (20.1%), and Hispanic (26.7%) students disproportionately stopped short, often leaving with no degree.
Special Education Status: Cramer’s V = 0.233, p < .001. Students with special education status were overwhelmingly concentrated in “Some college” (61.6%), with only 6.9% earning a bachelor’s or higher, compared to 41.4% of non-special education students.

Conclusion:
Demographic factors play a major role in shaping the highest credential attained. Economic disadvantage and special education status are the strongest barriers, sharply reducing the likelihood of earning a bachelor’s or higher degree. title: Post-secondary pathways
text:
High School Accomplishments
Key Findings:

ACT Composite Score: F(3, 19493) = 1165.82, p < .001. Students earning a bachelor’s or higher scored 3–4 points above those stopping at associate or sub-associate levels. “Some college” students had ACT scores similar to associate earners, suggesting non-completion is tied more to persistence than readiness.
PSEO Participation: Cramer’s V = 0.308, p < .001. PSEO participants were more than twice as likely to earn a bachelor’s or higher (50.5% vs. 22.2%) and far less likely to leave with “Some college” (23.9% vs. 44.9%). Associate and sub-associate outcomes were nearly identical between groups.
CTE Achievement: Cramer’s V = 0.140, p < .001. Concentrators/completors were less likely to earn bachelor’s+ (25.6%) and more likely to stop at associate (28.2%) or “Some college” (38.9%). Non-CTE students had the highest bachelor’s+ attainment (47%).
Total CTE Courses Taken: F(3, 28012) = 471.36, p < .001. Students who earned bachelor’s+ took fewer CTE courses, while those with sub-associate or “Some college” outcomes had taken more. Largest gap: bachelor’s+ vs. sub-associate, with >1.3 course difference.
MCA Math: F(3, 27568) = 925.88, p < .001. Bachelor’s+ earners scored 0.45–0.66 points higher than other groups. Lower scores characterized sub-associate and “Some college” outcomes.
MCA Reading: F(3, 27410) = 1053.96, p < .001. Bachelor’s+ earners scored 0.32–0.59 points higher than other groups, making reading one of the strongest predictors of higher attainment.
MCA Science: F(3, 22192) = 854.01, p < .001. Bachelor’s+ earners scored 0.41–0.60 points higher than other groups, while “Some college” and sub-associate students scored notably lower.

Conclusion:
High school accomplishments are among the most powerful predictors of the highest credential earned. PSEO participation stands out as the strongest programmatic factor, dramatically increasing the likelihood of bachelor’s or higher attainment. Academic performance (ACT, MCA Reading, and MCA Science especially) is tightly linked to ultimate attainment, differentiating bachelor’s+ earners from those who stop earlier. In contrast, greater CTE engagement (more courses and concentrator/completor status) is associated with lower levels of attainment, with students more likely to finish at the associate level or leave with “Some college.” Overall, rigorous academics and early postsecondary experiences strongly support higher credential attainment, while intensive CTE pathways align more with sub-baccalaureate outcomes.

Key Findings:
ANOVA: F(3, 19493) = 1165.82, p < .001.

Students who earned a bachelor’s degree or higher had ACT scores about 3.39 points higher than associate degree earners, and about 4.22 points higher than those who stopped short of an associate degree.
Students with less than an associate degree had significantly lower ACT scores than associate earners (–0.83).
Students in the “Some college” group scored similarly to associate earners (no significant difference).

Conclusion:
ACT performance is strongly associated with the highest credential attained. Higher ACT scores are linked to completing a bachelor’s or higher degree, while lower scores increase the likelihood of stopping short of an associate degree. Students who attended college without finishing a credential had ACT scores similar to associate earners, suggesting that non-completion is driven more by persistence factors than academic readiness alone.

title: Post-secondary pathways
text:
ps.grad.location
Tier 3 examined how demographic factors, high school characteristics, and high school accomplishments shape where students complete their postsecondary credentials: within their high school region, elsewhere in Minnesota, or outside the state.


Key Findings
Demographics

Economic Status: Economically disadvantaged students were more likely to graduate within their home region (67.8% vs. 55.7%), while non-disadvantaged students showed greater mobility, more often graduating elsewhere in MN or out of state.
Race/Ethnicity: American Indian (67.8%) and Hispanic (63.6%) graduates were most likely to stay in-region, while Asian/PI graduates were the least likely (48.7%), with higher rates graduating elsewhere in MN or out of state. White graduates showed a balanced pattern.
Special Education Status: Students with special education status were overwhelmingly more likely to remain in-region (73.8%) than non-special education students (57.7%), who were more mobile across the state and beyond.

High School Characteristics

School Locale: Rural graduates were less likely to remain in-region (38%) and more likely to graduate elsewhere in MN, while mixed/urban graduates were more likely to stay local (56–61%).
Economic Conditions: Students from lower-unemployment, higher-wage areas were more likely to graduate in their home region or outside the state, while those from higher-unemployment, lower-wage areas were more likely to complete elsewhere in Minnesota. Effects were modest but consistent.

High School Accomplishments

Academic Achievement (ACT & MCA scores): Students with higher ACT and MCA scores were significantly more likely to graduate elsewhere in Minnesota or out of state. Lower-scoring students were more likely to remain in-region.
PSEO Participation: Participants were more geographically mobile, with higher rates of completing elsewhere in Minnesota or outside the state, while non-participants were more likely to stay local.
CTE Engagement: Students with deeper CTE involvement (more courses, concentrator/completor status) were far more likely to graduate in-region, while students with little or no CTE experience showed greater mobility.




Overall Conclusion
Tier 3 results show that geographic mobility in postsecondary completion is closely tied to academic strength, program participation, and demographics.

Students who are academically stronger or PSEO participants are more likely to graduate away from their home region, either elsewhere in Minnesota or out of state.
Students who are economically disadvantaged, American Indian, Hispanic, or in special education, as well as those with deeper CTE engagement, are more likely to remain local.
Community economic conditions and school locale play smaller but notable roles, with rural and lower-wage contexts reinforcing regional completion.

In sum, Tier 3 highlights a divide between mobile, academically prepared students who pursue credentials beyond their home region, and students facing structural or programmatic constraints who are more likely to complete locally. This underscores the importance of academic preparation, resource access, and program opportunities in shaping not just whether students succeed in postsecondary, but where they do so.



Demographics
Key Findings:

Economic Status: Cramer’s V = 0.104, p < .001. Economically disadvantaged students were more likely to graduate within their high school region (67.8% vs. 55.7%), while non-disadvantaged students were more likely to graduate elsewhere in Minnesota (25.8% vs. 19.9%) or outside the state (18.5% vs. 12.3%).
Race/Ethnicity: Cramer’s V = 0.051, p < .001. American Indian (67.8%) and Hispanic (63.6%) graduates were most likely to remain in-region, while Asian/PI graduates were the least likely (48.7%), with higher rates completing elsewhere in MN (30.5%) or outside MN (20.8%). White graduates showed balanced outcomes across regions.
Special Education Status: Cramer’s V = 0.072, p < .001. Students with special education status were far more likely to remain in their high school region (73.8% vs. 57.7%), while non-special education students were more likely to complete elsewhere in MN (24.9% vs. 14.8%) or outside the state (17.4% vs. 11.4%).

Conclusion:
Demographic characteristics modestly influence the location of postsecondary graduation. Economically disadvantaged, American Indian, Hispanic, and special education students are more likely to stay within their home region, reflecting limited geographic mobility. In contrast, non-disadvantaged, White, and Asian/PI students show greater mobility, more often completing their credentials elsewhere in Minnesota or out of state. These differences suggest that resources, community ties, and support needs shape students’ ability or decision to pursue postsecondary opportunities beyond their home region.

Economic Status → Postsecondary Graduation Location (Ps.grad.location)Race/Ethnicity → Postsecondary Graduation Location (Ps.grad.location)Special Education Status → Postsecondary Graduation Location (Ps.grad.location)


Key Findings:
Chi-square = 202.79, Cramer’s V = 0.104, p < .001.

Economically disadvantaged students were more likely to graduate within their high school region (67.8%) compared to non-disadvantaged peers (55.7%).
Non-disadvantaged students were more likely to graduate elsewhere in Minnesota (25.8% vs. 19.9%) or outside the state (18.5% vs. 12.3%).

Conclusion:
Economic status is modestly associated with where students complete postsecondary credentials. Economically disadvantaged students tend to stay closer to home, graduating within their high school region, while non-disadvantaged students are more geographically mobile, more often completing credentials outside their region, both within and outside Minnesota.

title: Post-secondary pathways
text:
High School Characteristics
Key Findings:

School Locale (Dem_Desc): Cramer’s V = 0.113, p < .001. Graduates from entirely rural schools were less likely to remain in-region (38%) and more likely to graduate elsewhere in Minnesota (49.3%). Graduates from town/rural mix (55.9%) and urban/town/rural mix schools (61%) were more likely to stay in-region.
Average Unemployment Rate: F(2, 18642) = 19.17, p < .001. Graduates from lower-unemployment areas were slightly more likely to graduate in their home region or outside Minnesota, while graduates from higher-unemployment areas were more likely to graduate elsewhere in Minnesota.
Average Wages (as % of State Average): F(2, 18642) = 107.57, p < .001. Students from higher-wage areas were more likely to graduate either in their home region or outside the state, while those from lower-wage areas were more likely to graduate elsewhere in Minnesota.

Conclusion:
High school contextual characteristics exert a modest influence on where students complete postsecondary credentials. Locale matters somewhat, with rural students more likely to leave their region for other Minnesota institutions, while mixed/urban students are more likely to remain local. Economic conditions also play a role: students from stronger labor markets (lower unemployment, higher wages) are more likely to complete either locally or out of state, whereas weaker labor markets are tied to completion elsewhere in Minnesota. These effects are consistent but modest compared to demographic and accomplishment-based factors.

School Locale (Dem_Desc) → Postsecondary Graduation Location (Ps.grad.location)Average Unemployment Rate → Postsecondary Graduation Location (Ps.grad.location)Average Wages (as % of Minnesota State Average) → Postsecondary Graduation Location (Ps.grad.location)


Key Findings:
Chi-square = 472.32, Cramer’s V = 0.113, p < .001. Graduation location varied modestly by school locale:

Entirely rural graduates were more likely to complete outside their region (49.3% elsewhere in MN, 12.6% outside MN). Only 38% stayed within their high school region.
Town/rural mix graduates were much more likely to stay in-region (55.9%) and less likely to go outside the state (15.4%).
Urban/town/rural mix graduates were the most likely to remain in-region (61%) and the most likely to graduate outside MN (17.9%), with relatively fewer moving elsewhere in MN (21%).

Conclusion:
School locale shows a modest association with where students graduate from postsecondary institutions. Graduates from entirely rural schools are less likely to remain in-region and more likely to move elsewhere in Minnesota, while graduates from mixed or urban/town/rural schools are more likely to complete within their home region. These findings suggest that regional school context modestly shapes geographic mobility after high school graduation.

title: Post-secondary pathways
text:
High School Accomplishments
Key Findings:

ACT Composite Score: F(2, 14470) = 536.91, p < .001. Students who graduated elsewhere in Minnesota had the highest ACT scores, while those who graduated in-region or outside Minnesota had lower scores.
PSEO Participation: Cramer’s V = 0.117, p < .001. PSEO participants were more geographically mobile—less likely to graduate in-region (54% vs. 66%) and more likely to graduate elsewhere in Minnesota or outside the state.
CTE Achievement: Cramer’s V = 0.068, p < .001. CTE concentrators/completors were the most likely to remain in their high school region (65.8%) and the least likely to graduate outside MN (13.2%). Non-CTE students were the least likely to stay local and the most likely to graduate out of state.
Total CTE Courses Taken: F(2, 18642) = 63.26, p < .001. Students who stayed in-region had taken the most CTE courses, while those who graduated elsewhere in MN or out of state had taken fewer.
MCA Math: F(2, 18435) = 204.54, p < .001. Region graduates had significantly lower math scores than those who graduated elsewhere in MN or out of state.
MCA Reading: F(2, 18346) = 156.66, p < .001. Region graduates had significantly lower reading scores than elsewhere-in-MN and out-of-state graduates.
MCA Science: F(2, 14864) = 236.46, p < .001. Region graduates had significantly lower science scores than both elsewhere-in-MN and out-of-state graduates.

Conclusion:
High school accomplishments are strongly associated with postsecondary graduation location. Higher academic achievement (ACT and MCA scores) is linked to greater geographic mobility, with stronger students more likely to graduate elsewhere in Minnesota or out of state. PSEO participation also increases mobility, while CTE engagement (more courses and concentrator/completor status) anchors students closer to home, with higher rates of in-region graduation. Overall, academic strength and dual-enrollment experiences encourage mobility, while CTE pathways reinforce regional ties.

title: Post-secondary pathways
text:
Tier 1: Core Access and Attainment

Demographics were the strongest and most consistent predictors. Economic disadvantage, race/ethnicity (especially American Indian, Black, and Hispanic students), and special education status all reduced likelihood of enrollment, attendance, and completion.
High School Characteristics (locale, local unemployment, wages) had weak and inconsistent effects.
High School Accomplishments were powerful predictors. Higher ACT/MCA scores and PSEO participation strongly boosted immediate enrollment, persistence, and graduation. In contrast, greater CTE engagement was associated with lower enrollment and graduation, aligning with workforce entry rather than postsecondary continuation.

title: Post-secondary pathways
section: Tier 2: Type of Postsecondary Experience (Highest Credential Earned)
text:
Tier 2: Type of Postsecondary Experience (Highest Credential Earned)

Economic disadvantage and special education status created the steepest barriers to earning a bachelor’s or higher degree, with these groups concentrated in “Some college” or sub-associate credentials.
Racial disparities persisted: White and Asian/PI students were far more likely to complete bachelor’s or graduate degrees, while American Indian, Black, and Hispanic students were more likely to stop at associate’s or leave with no credential.
Academic readiness and PSEO participation were the strongest positive predictors of bachelor’s+ attainment. Students with higher ACT/MCA scores and PSEO experience were much more likely to progress to advanced credentials.
CTE engagement again tracked with sub-baccalaureate attainment, with concentrators/completors more likely to finish with associate’s or stop at “Some college.”

title: Post-secondary pathways
text:
Tier 3: Location of Postsecondary Graduation

Demographics shaped mobility: disadvantaged, American Indian, Hispanic, and special education students were most likely to graduate within their high school region, while non-disadvantaged, White, and Asian/PI students showed greater mobility (elsewhere in MN or out-of-state).
High school characteristics mattered modestly. Rural students tended to leave their region but stay within Minnesota, while students from stronger labor markets (lower unemployment, higher wages) were more likely to graduate in-region or out-of-state.
Accomplishments mattered most: Higher ACT/MCA scores and PSEO participation were strongly tied to graduating outside the home region, while heavier CTE engagement (more courses, concentrator/completor status) was associated with staying local.

title: Pathways taken after high school - Northeast
text:
Special Education Status
Key Findings
There is a statistically significant relationship between Special Education status and post-graduation outcomes in all three timeframes:

1 year after graduation: χ²(4) = 3110.70, Cramer’s V = 0.258, p < .001, N = 46,777

5 years after graduation: χ²(4) = 829.87, Cramer’s V = 0.155, p < .001, N = 34,683

10 years after graduation: χ²(3) = 231.15, Cramer’s V = 0.108, p < .001, N = 19,828

The strength of association is strongest in the first year and weakens over time, but the relationship remains significant. The primary pattern is that SpecialEd students are less likely to attend postsecondary and more likely to be in not meaningful or disconnected outcomes. While regional meaningful employment is roughly equal at Year 1, by Years 5 and 10 non-SpecialEd students pull ahead in meaningful employment in the region.
Interpretation Over Time
1 Year After Graduation: Regional meaningful employment is nearly the same for SpecialEd (15.6%) and non-SpecialEd (15.3%). The sharpest differences are in education and disconnection: only 21.4% of SpecialEd students are attending postsecondary compared to 52.5% of non-SpecialEd, and 25.1% of SpecialEd students are disconnected compared to 9.3% of non-SpecialEd. This points to an early divergence where SpecialEd students are disproportionately outside of education and tracked employment.
5 Years After Graduation: Gaps in regional meaningful employment begin to open (SpecialEd 24.6% vs. non-SpecialEd 26.8%). SpecialEd students are still much less likely to be in postsecondary (6.8% vs. 17.6%) and more likely to be not meaningful (29.1% vs. 20.0%) or disconnected (30.0% vs. 19.5%). By this stage, non-SpecialEd students strengthen their advantage in both education and regional meaningful jobs.
10 Years After Graduation: The gap in regional meaningful employment widens further (SpecialEd 24.7% vs. non-SpecialEd 29.9%). Non-SpecialEd students are also more likely to be in meaningful employment statewide (20.6% vs. 11.7%). SpecialEd students remain more concentrated in disconnected outcomes (36.9% vs. 31.7%). The long-term trajectory shows that SpecialEd students are less attached to meaningful regional work and face persistent disadvantages in education and quality employment.

title: Pathways After High School – Northeast Minnesota
text:
This one-page overview integrates effect size tables, key insights, and a visual comparison chart across all four major sections of analysis.




Demographics
- Strongest predictor: SpecialEd Status (V = 0.258, Yr 1).
- Demographics fade in importance over time; SpecialEd and Race/Ethnicity remain the most relevant.
High School Characteristics
- Local economic conditions (unemployment, wages) significantly shape early outcomes (F = 53.1 for unemployment, Yr 1).
- Rural/urban divides also matter, but effects diminish by Year 10.
High School Accomplishments
- Academic/college-prep measures (ACT, MCA, PSEO, AP) → statewide pathways, less regional attachment.
- CTE achievement and course load → strongest predictors of regional meaningful employment.
- MCA Math has the largest overall predictive power (F = 1344.5, Yr 1).
Postsecondary Experiences
- The most powerful overall predictors.
- Attendance and graduation separate students into statewide vs. regional pathways.
- Credential level and location nuance outcomes: regional/2-year credentials anchor locally, 4-year/out-of-state expand mobility.







Effect Sizes Overview







Regional meaningful employment is most strongly tied to CTE in high school and regional/2-year postsecondary pathways.

Statewide employment and mobility stem from academic success and 4-year/out-of-state credentials.

Disconnection is concentrated among non-attenders, non-graduates, and those with weaker preparation, amplified by local economic stressors.

This highlights a dual pathway model:
1. Academic + 4-year trajectories → statewide mobility and higher credentials.
2. CTE + regional PS pathways → strong anchoring in the local workforce.
Both are vital in shaping Northeast Minnesota’s labor market outcomes.

Postsecondary enrollment remains somewhat higher (17.3% vs. 15.7%), while not meaningful and disconnection outcomes are slightly lower for Range graduates (19.6% vs. 21.7% and 19.3% vs. 21.5%)【488†source】.
10 Years After Graduation: The gap in regional meaningful employment becomes more pronounced: 34.0% of Range graduates vs. 28.0% of non‑Range graduates. Range graduates maintain comparable statewide meaningful employment (18.4% vs. 19.7%), and their disconnection remains modestly lower (29.7% vs. 33.1%)【489†source】. The long‑term trend indicates that Range school students are more attached to regional meaningful work than non‑Range peers.

title: Pathways taken after high school - Northeast
text:
Average County Unemployment Rate (Sophomore–Senior Years)
Key Findings
There is a statistically significant relationship between the county unemployment rate during high school and post‑graduation outcomes in all three timeframes (ANOVA on unemployment rate across outcome groups):

1 year after graduation: F(4, 46772) = 12.55, p < .001

5 years after graduation: F(4, 34678) = 13.03, p < .001

10 years after graduation: F(3, 19745) = 9.69, p < .001

Effects are modest but reliable across years.
Interpretation Over Time (Tukey HSD highlights)
Year 1:
- Attending postsecondary comes from higher‑unemployment counties than Meaningful employment in the region (Δ = +0.118, p < .001).
- Not meaningful and No MN record are also higher than Meaningful region (Δ ≈ +0.07 to +0.08, both p < .05).
- Takeaway: in the first year, regional meaningful employment is associated with comparatively lower local unemployment than several alternative pathways.
Year 5:
- Meaningful MN (statewide) > Meaningful region (Δ = +0.146, p < .001).
- Attending ps and No MN record are lower than Meaningful MN (Δ ≈ −0.091 and −0.088, both p ≤ .004).
- Takeaway: by five years out, statewide meaningful employment is associated with higher‑unemployment counties than regional meaningful jobs, while continued schooling and no record skew lower than statewide meaningful.
Year 10:
- Meaningful MN > Meaningful region (Δ = +0.088, p = .0009).
- Not meaningful > Meaningful region (Δ = +0.067, p = .022).
- No MN record < Meaningful MN and < Not meaningful (Δ = −0.103 and −0.082; p ≤ .002).
- Takeaway: a decade out, regional meaningful employment remains linked to lower unemployment contexts than statewide meaningful and not meaningful routes; those with no MN record tend to come from lower‑unemployment counties than peers in statewide/not‑meaningful outcomes.
Overall, the pattern suggests that students from lower‑unemployment counties are more likely to land in meaningful employment within the region, whereas higher‑unemployment origins are more often associated with statewide meaningful, not meaningful, or continued schooling pathways.

title: Model-Ready Variable Recommendations
text:
As we move from descriptive analysis to predictive modeling, the goal is to retain the strongest predictors while removing weaker or redundant ones.
Below is a structured list by section.



Keep / Prioritize
- SpecialEd Status (strongest demographic predictor)
- Race/Ethnicity (moderate strength, important equity covariate)
Drop / Deprioritize
- Gender (weak, V ≈ .05–.10, fades over time)
- English Learner (very weak, V < .07, small group sizes)
- Economic Status (moderate but weaker compared to later predictors; may retain as a control if needed)




Keep / Prioritize
- Dem_Desc (Rural/Urban) – moderate, useful contextual control
- Avg. Unemployment – strong early F-values, local context matters
- Avg. Wages % State – strong F-values, economic environment indicator
Drop / Deprioritize
- Range School (very weak effect, V ≈ .03–.05)




Keep / Prioritize
- ACT (took ACT, ACT Composite Score) – strong, differentiates pathways
- MCA (Math strongest, Reading & Science secondary) – critical academic predictors
- CTE Achievement – anchors to regional meaningful employment
- Total CTE Courses Taken – consistent predictor of regional attachment
- PSEO Participation – strong early differentiator of statewide vs regional pathways
Drop / Deprioritize
- SAT Taken (consistently weak, V ≈ .07, redundant with ACT)
- AP Exam (moderate, but less powerful than ACT/MCA; may be dropped if multicollinearity is high)




Keep / Prioritize
- Attended Postsecondary Within First Year – strongest early effect (V > .5)
- Ever Attended Postsecondary – very strong differentiator (V > .6)
- Postsecondary Graduation – critical predictor of long-term stability
- Highest Credential Level – strong differentiator between statewide vs regional pathways
- Graduation Location – strong anchor for regional vs statewide attachment
Drop / Deprioritize
- Institution Sector – moderate only (V ≈ .14–.16); may be redundant with credential level & location





Drop: Gender, English Learner, Range School, SAT Taken, possibly AP Exam, possibly Institution Sector

Keep: All others, with focus on SpecialEd, Race/Ethnicity, local economic indicators, ACT/MCA, CTE, and Postsecondary attendance/graduation/credentials.

This balances parsimony (leaner model) with coverage (keeping conceptually important drivers of outcomes).

title: Pathways taken after high school - Northeast
text:
CTE Achievement
Key Findings
There is a statistically significant relationship between CTE achievement (Concentrator/Completer, Participant, No CTE) and post‑graduation outcomes across all three timeframes:

1 year after graduation: χ²(8) = 508.14, Cramer’s V = 0.074, p < .001, N = 46,777【663†source】

5 years after graduation: χ²(8) = 307.50, Cramer’s V = 0.067, p < .001, N = 34,683【664†source】

10 years after graduation: χ²(6) = 174.53, Cramer’s V = 0.066, p < .001, N = 19,828【665†source】

The associations are modest but consistent. The clearest relationship is that CTE Concentrators/Completers are more likely to enter meaningful employment in the region, while students with no CTE are more likely to be in postsecondary or outside regional attachment.
Interpretation Over Time
1 Year After Graduation: Regional meaningful employment is highest for CTE Concentrators/Completers (19.4%), compared to Participants (15.1%) and No CTE students (12.6%). Postsecondary enrollment is much higher among No CTE (51.3%) and Participants (49.2%) than Concentrators/Completers (41.5%). This suggests that CTE pathways steer students more quickly into regional work while non‑CTE students delay employment through postsecondary【663†source】.
5 Years After Graduation: The regional employment gap persists: 31.9% for Concentrators/Completers vs. 27.2% for Participants and 22.9% for No CTE. Postsecondary attendance is relatively low across all groups (13–17%), but still higher for those without CTE. Concentrators/Completers maintain stronger local employment connections, while non‑CTE students lean slightly more toward statewide employment (15.7%)【664†source】.
10 Years After Graduation: Regional meaningful employment remains strongest among Concentrators/Completers (34.6%), compared to Participants (29.1%) and No CTE students (25.5%). Statewide meaningful employment is more evenly distributed, while disconnection is highest among those with No CTE (35.5%). The long‑term pattern confirms that CTE achievement reinforces regional employment pathways, while students outside CTE are more likely to leave the region or experience disconnection【665†source】.
Overall, CTE achievement consistently predicts stronger regional workforce attachment, distinguishing Concentrators/Completers as the group most likely to remain engaged in meaningful employment within the region over time.

title: Pathways taken after high school - Northeast
text:
MCA Science (MCA.S)
Key Findings
There is a statistically significant relationship between MCA Science scores and post‑graduation outcomes in all three timeframes (ANOVA across outcome groups):

1 year after graduation: F(4, 37501) = 544.02, p < .001

5 years after graduation: F(4, 26050) = 160.29, p < .001

10 years after graduation: F(3, 11879) = 81.74, p < .001

The results show a very strong early effect that remains significant through 10 years. The key pattern is that higher MCA Science scores are associated with postsecondary education and statewide meaningful employment, while lower scores are tied to regional meaningful employment or not meaningful outcomes.
Interpretation Over Time (Tukey HSD highlights)
Year 1:
- Postsecondary attendees score substantially higher than regional meaningful (+0.38, p < .001).
- Statewide meaningful (+0.07) also scores higher than regional meaningful (p = .025).
- Not meaningful (−0.07) and No MN record (−0.12) score below postsecondary.
- Takeaway: early on, regional meaningful work is tied to lower MCA-S scores, while education and statewide jobs are tied to higher scores.
Year 5:
- Statewide meaningful (+0.25) and postsecondary (+0.32) are far above regional meaningful (p < .001).
- No MN record (+0.11) is also higher.
- Not meaningful (−0.04) is slightly below regional meaningful (p = .044).
- Takeaway: by 5 years, the gap widens, with statewide and postsecondary pathways clearly tied to higher MCA-S scores, while regional meaningful remains lower.
Year 10:
- Statewide meaningful (+0.27) and No MN record (+0.18) score above regional meaningful (p < .001).
- Not meaningful (−0.31) scores well below regional meaningful (p < .001).
- Takeaway: a decade out, regional meaningful employment remains linked to lower MCA-S scores, while higher scores push students into statewide jobs or out of tracked MN employment.
Overall, MCA Science mirrors the MCA Reading pattern: academic achievement is strongly tied to educational and statewide pathways, while lower achievement is associated with stronger regional attachment or risk of weaker employment outcomes.

title: Pathways taken after high school - Northeast
text:
SAT Test Participation (SAT Taken)
Key Findings
There is a statistically significant relationship between taking the SAT and post-graduation outcomes in all three timeframes:

1 year after graduation: χ²(4) = 228.74, Cramer’s V = 0.070, p < .001, N = 46,777【595†source】

5 years after graduation: χ²(4) = 188.76, Cramer’s V = 0.074, p < .001, N = 34,683【596†source】

10 years after graduation: χ²(3) = 99.99, Cramer’s V = 0.071, p < .001, N = 19,828【597†source】

The effect sizes are small but consistent. The key pattern is that SAT takers are far more likely to attend postsecondary education, while non‑takers are more likely to enter meaningful employment in the region.
Interpretation Over Time
1 Year After Graduation: SAT takers are overwhelmingly in postsecondary (73.5% vs. 47.3% for non‑takers). Regional meaningful employment is much lower for SAT takers (3.2% vs. 15.5%), while disconnection is also somewhat lower (9.0% vs. 11.7%)【595†source】.
5 Years After Graduation: SAT takers maintain higher postsecondary enrollment (30.1% vs. 15.8%). Regional meaningful employment is still much lower (7.6% vs. 26.8%). Interestingly, SAT takers are slightly more likely to be in meaningful employment statewide (18.2% vs. 15.1%). Disconnection is higher among SAT takers (28.6% vs. 20.9%)【596†source】.
10 Years After Graduation: SAT takers continue to show very low regional meaningful employment (11.5% vs. 29.5%), while statewide meaningful employment is similar (18.6% vs. 19.4%). Disconnection is much higher among SAT takers (55.9% vs. 32.0%)【597†source】.
Overall, SAT participation identifies a small group of students who overwhelmingly pursue postsecondary initially, but long‑term outcomes show weak regional attachment and much higher disconnection, suggesting that SAT takers may be more mobile, pursue opportunities outside the region or state, or leave tracked employment systems altogether.

title: Pathways taken after high school - Northeast
text:
Post-Secondary Enrollment Options (PSEO) Participation
Key Findings
There is a statistically significant relationship between PSEO participation and post-graduation outcomes in all three timeframes:

1 year after graduation: χ²(4) = 3076.21, Cramer’s V = 0.290, p < .001, N = 36,625【542†source】

5 years after graduation: χ²(4) = 430.00, Cramer’s V = 0.132, p < .001, N = 24,531【543†source】

10 years after graduation: χ²(3) = 77.28, Cramer’s V = 0.089, p < .001, N = 9,676【544†source】

The strength of association is very strong in the first year but weakens considerably over time. The primary relationship is that PSEO participants are much more likely to pursue postsecondary education, while non‑participants are more likely to enter meaningful regional employment early on.
Interpretation Over Time
1 Year After Graduation: Regional meaningful employment is higher among non‑PSEO students (18.4%) compared to PSEO participants (12.6%). In contrast, PSEO participants are far more likely to be attending postsecondary (61.8% vs. 33.6%). Disconnection is notably lower among PSEO participants (6.5% vs. 16.2%)【542†source】.
5 Years After Graduation: Regional meaningful employment gaps narrow (28.1% non‑PSEO vs. 25.1% PSEO). Importantly, PSEO participants surpass non‑participants in meaningful employment statewide (18.0% vs. 13.3%). Postsecondary attendance is higher among PSEO students (19.1% vs. 11.9%), while disconnection is lower (18.7% vs. 23.5%)【543†source】.
10 Years After Graduation: Regional meaningful employment is relatively similar (29.7% non‑PSEO vs. 26.8% PSEO). PSEO participants maintain higher statewide meaningful employment (24.0% vs. 16.9%), while disconnection rates are similar (~32%). The long‑term pattern suggests PSEO participants transition from education into statewide meaningful jobs, while non‑participants retain an edge in regional meaningful employment【544†source】.

title: Pathways taken after high school - Northeast
text:
MCA Reading (MCA.R)
Key Findings
There is a statistically significant relationship between MCA Reading scores and post‑graduation outcomes in all three timeframes (ANOVA across outcome groups):

1 year after graduation: F(4, 42500) = 689.45, p < .001

5 years after graduation: F(4, 31013) = 119.45, p < .001

10 years after graduation: F(3, 17590) = 237.15, p < .001

The results show a very strong early effect that remains significant over time. The primary pattern is that higher MCA Reading scores are associated with postsecondary enrollment and statewide meaningful employment, while lower scores are more tied to regional meaningful employment or not meaningful/disconnected outcomes.
Interpretation Over Time (Tukey HSD highlights)
Year 1:
- Postsecondary attendees score about +0.26 higher than regional meaningful workers (p < .001).
- Not meaningful (+0.09) and No MN record (+0.14) also score higher than regional meaningful (p ≤ .02).
- Takeaway: regional meaningful employment is linked to lower reading scores, while higher scores track into postsecondary and other categories.
Year 5:
- Postsecondary (+0.21), statewide meaningful (+0.17), and No MN record (+0.08) all score above regional meaningful (p < .001).
- Not meaningful scores slightly below regional meaningful (−0.17, p < .001).
- Takeaway: by five years, regional meaningful employment sits lower on the MCA-R spectrum, while postsecondary and statewide jobs skew higher.
Year 10:
- Statewide meaningful (+0.18) and No MN record (+0.14) are significantly above regional meaningful (p < .001).
- Not meaningful scores considerably lower (−0.25, p < .001).
- Takeaway: a decade out, regional meaningful employment remains tied to lower MCA-R scores, with higher scores concentrated in statewide meaningful employment or outside tracked records.
Overall, MCA Reading reinforces that academic achievement predicts longer-term educational and statewide work pathways, while lower scores are associated with stronger regional attachment but also greater risk of not meaningful outcomes.

title: Pathways taken after high school - Northeast
text:
AP Exam Participation
Key Findings
There is a statistically significant relationship between AP exam participation and post-graduation outcomes in all three timeframes:

1 year after graduation: χ²(4) = 822.44, Cramer’s V = 0.133, p < .001, N = 46,777【581†source】

5 years after graduation: χ²(4) = 301.32, Cramer’s V = 0.093, p < .001, N = 34,683【582†source】

10 years after graduation: χ²(3) = 113.60, Cramer’s V = 0.076, p < .001, N = 19,828【583†source】

The strength of association is strongest in the first year and declines over time, though remains statistically significant. The primary relationship is that AP exam participants are much more likely to attend postsecondary, while non‑participants are more likely to enter meaningful regional employment.
Interpretation Over Time
1 Year After Graduation: Regional meaningful employment is substantially higher among non‑AP students (16.1% vs. 7.7%), while AP exam participants are much more likely to be in postsecondary (68.8% vs. 45.7%). Disconnection is lower for AP participants (6.7% vs. 12.2%)【581†source】.
5 Years After Graduation: Non‑AP students retain an advantage in regional meaningful employment (27.4% vs. 17.1%), while AP participants show higher rates of statewide meaningful employment (19.8% vs. 14.7%) and continued postsecondary enrollment (23.7% vs. 15.3%). Disconnection rates are similar (~21%)【582†source】.
10 Years After Graduation: Regional meaningful employment remains higher for non‑AP students (29.9% vs. 22.7%). AP participants hold an advantage in statewide meaningful employment (27.0% vs. 18.7%). Disconnection is slightly higher for AP participants (36.0% vs. 32.1%), suggesting some trade‑off in regional attachment over time【583†source】.
Overall, AP exam participation sorts students into pathways favoring education and statewide employment, while non‑participants maintain stronger ties to regional meaningful employment.

title: Pathways taken after high school - Northeast
text:
Postsecondary Graduation by Institution Sector (ps.grad.InstitutionSector)
Key Findings
There is a statistically significant relationship between the sector of postsecondary graduation (4‑year public, 2‑year public, other) and post‑graduation outcomes across all timeframes:

1 year after graduation: χ²(12) = 1313.46, Cramer’s V = 0.138, p < .001, N = 22,962【748†source】

5 years after graduation: χ²(12) = 1181.64, Cramer’s V = 0.152, p < .001, N = 17,154【749†source】

10 years after graduation: χ²(6) = 498.68, Cramer’s V = 0.160, p < .001, N = 9,691【750†source】

The relationship is moderate but consistent, strengthening slightly by year 10. The main divide is between 4‑year and 2‑year graduates, with different propensities toward statewide vs. regional employment.
Interpretation Over Time
Year 1: Almost all graduates remain in postsecondary, but small differences emerge. 2‑year graduates show the highest early regional employment (20.6%), compared to 7.1% among “other” graduates and just 4.5% among 4‑year graduates. Graduates of 4‑year and “other” institutions overwhelmingly remain enrolled (86%+), delaying workforce entry【748†source】.
Year 5: Clearer differences appear. 2‑year graduates lead in regional meaningful employment (40.7%), while 4‑year graduates show higher statewide employment (21.8%). “Other” graduates also lean toward regional work (21.7%). Disconnection rates are somewhat higher among 4‑year graduates, but overall the trend is that 2‑year pathways support stronger early attachment to regional jobs【749†source】.
Year 10: By this point, differences remain. 2‑year graduates sustain the highest regional meaningful employment (45.1%), while 4‑year graduates lean toward statewide meaningful employment (29.5%). “Other” graduates remain in the middle with balanced outcomes. Importantly, no‑record rates are lowest for 2‑year graduates (21.6%), suggesting stronger regional retention. In contrast, 4‑year graduates have higher statewide outcomes but also higher “no record” rates (33.6%)【750†source】.
Overall, institution sector matters: 2‑year graduates show stronger long‑term regional employment, while 4‑year graduates pursue statewide opportunities and are more mobile, and “other” graduates fall between.

Postsecondary experiences draw a clear line between regional anchoring vs. statewide mobility.

2. Absence of postsecondary pathways results in earlier regional employment but higher long‑term vulnerability.
3. The type, level, and location of postsecondary attainment nuance this divide: regional and 2‑year pathways strengthen local attachment, while higher‑level and out‑of‑region pathways expand opportunities but reduce regional ties.

title: Pathways taken after high school - Northeast
text:
Highest Credential Level (highest.cred.level)
Key Findings
There is a statistically significant relationship between highest credential earned and post‑graduation outcomes across all timeframes:

1 year after graduation: χ²(20) = 25,119.08, Cramer’s V = 0.366, p < .001, N = 46,777【760†source】

5 years after graduation: χ²(20) = 7,371.79, Cramer’s V = 0.231, p < .001, N = 34,683【761†source】

10 years after graduation: χ²(12) = 1,030.86, Cramer’s V = 0.132, p < .001, N = 19,828【762†source】

The association is strong in the first year, moderates by year 5, and weakens further by year 10, though it remains significant. The key distinction is that higher credentials (Bachelor’s or above) delay regional employment but lead to stronger statewide employment later, while lower or mid‑level credentials (Associate, less than Associate) are more tied to early and sustained regional employment.
Interpretation Over Time
Year 1: Students with no college are most likely to be in regional meaningful employment (19.9%), but also heavily represented in disconnection categories (44.2% not meaningful, 30.1% no record). Those with some college or Associate degrees show moderate regional employment (18–19%) but are strongly concentrated in “attending PS” (49–69%). Students pursuing a Bachelor’s or higher overwhelmingly remain in education (86.5%) and show the lowest regional employment (5.7%)【760†source】.
Year 5: Regional meaningful employment peaks among less than Associate (42.3%) and Associate degree earners (36.5%), with some college also relatively strong (29.2%). By contrast, Bachelor’s or higher show lower regional attachment (19.1%) but higher statewide meaningful employment (20.5%). Non‑college individuals still show significant disconnection (27.4% not meaningful, 37.0% no record)【761†source】.
Year 10: The regional advantage of Associate and sub‑Associate credentials remains high (42–43%), while Bachelor’s or higher show stronger statewide employment (27.9%) and lower regional employment (26.5%). Non‑college individuals continue to show the weakest outcomes, with the highest disconnection rates (41.7% no record)【762†source】.
Overall, the evidence shows that mid‑level credentials (Associate and below) strongly anchor individuals in regional employment, while Bachelor’s and above foster statewide mobility and stronger longer‑term outcomes, and no credential consistently yields the weakest employment stability.

title: Pathways taken after high school - Northeast
text:
Postsecondary Graduation Location (ps.grad.location)
Key Findings
There is a statistically significant relationship between location of postsecondary graduation and post‑graduation outcomes across all timeframes:

Interpretation Over Time
Year 1: Regional graduates show the strongest immediate tie to local jobs, with 65.8% in regional meaningful employment, compared to 23.8% of non‑graduates, 28.7% of MN graduates outside the region, and 22.0% of graduates outside MN. Non‑graduates are most often disconnected (43.4% “not meaningful” and 25.9% “no record”)【772†source】.
Year 5: Regional graduates remain highly concentrated in regional employment (50.2%), far above MN graduates outside the region (18.3%) or graduates outside MN (20.4%). By contrast, MN graduates outside the region have the highest statewide employment (44.0%), reflecting mobility within the state. Non‑graduates remain more disconnected (28.4% “not meaningful” and 31.0% “no record”)【773†source】.
Year 10: Regional graduates sustain a long‑term edge in local employment (43.1%), while MN graduates outside the region remain more mobile (38.0% in statewide employment). Graduates outside MN have lower regional (20.7%) and statewide (17.8%) employment, with a higher share of disconnection (49.4% “no record”). Non‑graduates remain the weakest group, with only 25.6% regional employment and the highest share of disconnection (36.7% “no record”)【774†source】.
Overall, the evidence shows that regional PS graduation strongly anchors individuals in the local workforce, while graduation outside the region or outside MN promotes mobility and statewide attachment. Non‑graduates remain at the greatest risk of disconnection across all timeframes.
